title: Bagging vs Boosting
text: Say it in 30s: Both are ensembles of many models, but they attack different errors. Bagging trains many strong, high-variance models (e.g. deep trees) in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them — it reduces variance . Boosting trains weak, high-bias models (e.g. shallow trees) sequentially, each correcting the previous one s mistakes — it mainly reduces bias (and some variance). Bagging (e.g. Random Forest) Independent trees on resampled data; predictions averaged/voted. Random Forest adds feature subsampling to decorrelate trees. Robust, parallelizable, hard to overfit by adding trees. Boosting (e.g. AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost/LightGBM) Each learner focuses on the residuals/errors of the ensemble so far. Often the strongest tabular performers, but more tuning and can overfit if over-trained. Sequential → less parallelizable. One-liner: bagging = many independent opinions averaged (variance↓); boosting = a relay team fixing each other s mistakes (bias↓). See depth: Classification Methods (§6–7). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Overfitting Underfitting .

title: Classification Methods
heads: The Master Table — Every Classifier Side by Side
Naive Bayes — Fast and Great for Text
k-NN and SVM — Distance vs Margin
Trees, Forests, Boosting — Bagging vs Boosting
text: Classification — predicting a discrete label — is the single most common framing you ll be asked to reason about, and interviewers use it to probe whether you understand why one model beats another on a given dataset, not just how to call .fit() . We line every major classifier up side by side, split them into the two families that organize the whole field, then walk each one with its assumptions, strengths, and the questions it tends to attract. What you #39;ll be able to say after this chapter Place any classifier in the generative vs discriminative split and say what it learns. Derive logistic regression from the log-odds and explain why it s the default baseline. Explain why Naive Bayes works despite a naive assumption that s almost always false . Contrast bagging vs boosting in one sentence and say which fights bias vs variance. Pick a classifier from the shape of the data: size, dimensionality, linearity, interpretability. # The Master Table — Every Classifier Side by Side Before any single method, hold the landscape in your head. The classifiers you ll be asked about differ along a few axes that actually predict their behavior: what they learn, whether the boundary is linear, how they scale, and how interpretable they are. Model Family Boundary Strengths Watch out for Logistic regression Discriminative Linear Usually well-calibrated probabilities, interpretable, fast Underfits nonlinear data Naive Bayes Generative Linear in log-space (multinomial/Bernoulli; Gaussian NB can be quadratic) Tiny data, text, very fast Independence assumption, poor calibration k-NN Discriminative (lazy) Nonlinear No training, simple Slow at predict, curse of dimensionality SVM Discriminative Linear or kernel Strong in high-dim, margin-based Slow on big data, no native probabilities Decision tree Discriminative Axis-aligned Interpretable, handles mixed types Overfits, unstable Random forest Discriminative (bagging) Nonlinear Robust, low tuning, strong default Larger, less interpretable Gradient boosting Discriminative (boosting) Nonlinear Often best on tabular Tuning-sensitive, slower to train Neural network Discriminative Arbitrary Crushes vision/text/audio Data-hungry, opaque, tuning Memory hook Two questions sort almost any classifier: does it model the data (generative) or just the boundary (discriminative)? and is the boundary a straight line or can it bend? Everything else is a footnote on cost and interpretability. Interview angle Walk me through which classifier you d try. Don t recite — reason from the data. The senior move: name a fast linear baseline (logistic regression), then a strong nonlinear default (gradient-boosted trees for tabular, a neural net for perceptual data), and justify each by the data s structure. Jumping straight to XGBoost without a baseline reads as junior. # Two Families: Generative vs Discriminative This split organizes the entire chapter, so it s worth one clean restatement. A discriminative model learns the boundary directly — p ( y ∣ x ) p(y \mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) , or just where the line goes. A generative model learns how each class produces data — p ( x ∣ y ) p(x \mid y) p ( x ∣ y ) and p ( y ) p(y) p ( y ) — then flips it with Bayes rule to classify. Discriminative Generative Learns p ( y ∣ x ) p(y \mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) — the boundary p ( x , y ) = p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) p(x, y) = p(x \mid y)\,p(y) p ( x , y ) = p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) — the full story Classifies by Which side of the line? Which class most likely generated this x x x ? Can sample / detect outliers? No Yes Data appetite Wants more data, hits lower error Works on small data if assumptions hold Examples Logistic regression, SVM, trees, NN Naive Bayes, GMM, LDA, HMM The practical takeaway is the Ng–Jordan result from Fundamentals : a generative model reaches its error floor with fewer samples but that floor is higher ; the matching discriminative model is slower to converge but ends up more accurate with enough data. So generative shines in the small-data regime, discriminative in the large-data regime. Memory hook Discriminative asks which side? Generative asks who made this? — it learns each class s recipe and picks the most plausible cook. # Logistic Regression — The Must-Know Baseline Despite the name, logistic regression is a classifier . It s the single most important model to be able to derive from scratch, because nearly every interview that touches classification touches it. The setup: a linear model produces a score z = w ⊤ x + b z = w^\top x + b z = w ⊤ x + b that lives anywhere on the real line, but a probability has to sit in [ 0 , 1 ] [0, 1] [ 0 , 1 ] . The sigmoid squashes it: σ ( z ) = 1 1 + e − z \sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} σ ( z ) = 1 + e − z 1 ​ . Read backwards, this says the model is linear in the log-odds : log ⁡ p 1 − p = w ⊤ x + b \log\frac{p}{1 - p} = w^\top x + b lo g 1 − p p ​ = w ⊤ x + b That single fact is the heart of the method — a one-unit change in a feature shifts the log-odds by its weight. It s trained by minimizing cross-entropy (log-loss), not squared error. The reason matters and gets asked: cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood under a Bernoulli model, it s convex in the weights (so any local optimum is global; with separable data the weights diverge unless regularized), and it punishes confident wrong predictions hard. Squared error on a sigmoid is non-convex and produces vanishing gradients when the model is confidently wrong — exactly when you most need a signal. Property Logistic regression Why it matters Output Usually well-calibrated probability Threshold it for any precision/recall tradeoff Boundary Linear in features Add interactions/polynomials for curves Loss Cross-entropy (convex) Global optimum, clean gradients Regularization L1 (sparse) or L2 (shrink) Controls overfitting, L1 selects features Memory hook Logistic regression is linear regression on the log-odds , then squashed by a sigmoid. Linear in log-odds, probability out. Interview angle Three near-certain questions: (1) Why sigmoid? — to map a real-valued score to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] [ 0 , 1 ] and make it linear in log-odds. (2) Why cross-entropy not MSE? — convexity + non-vanishing gradients + it s the Bernoulli MLE. (3) Is it linear? — the boundary is linear in features, even though the sigmoid is nonlinear. Getting (3) right separates people who memorized from people who understand. Go deeper (optional) For multiclass, logistic regression generalizes to softmax (multinomial) regression: one weight vector per class, normalized to a distribution. Softmax + cross-entropy is exactly the output layer of most neural-net classifiers — so what s the last layer of a classifier net? is the same idea you already know. # Naive Bayes — Fast and Great for Text Naive Bayes is the canonical generative classifier and a perennial interview favorite because its central paradox is so clean: it rests on an assumption that is almost always false, and it works anyway. It applies Bayes rule — p ( y ∣ x ) ∝ p ( y ) p ( x ∣ y ) p(y \mid x) \propto p(y)\,p(x \mid y) p ( y ∣ x ) ∝ p ( y ) p ( x ∣ y ) — and makes the naive assumption that all features are conditionally independent given the class. That lets it factor p ( x ∣ y ) p(x \mid y) p ( x ∣ y ) into a product of per-feature terms, which is why it trains in a single pass and handles tens of thousands of features (every word in a vocabulary) effortlessly. The assumption is obviously wrong — in text, New and York are not independent. But Naive Bayes only needs the correct class to get the highest score , not accurate probabilities. The dependencies often distort all classes scores in the same direction, so the argmax survives even when the probabilities themselves are badly miscalibrated. That s the resolution to the paradox, and the answer interviewers want. Variant Use on Models each feature as Multinomial NB Word counts (text) Count from a multinomial Bernoulli NB Binary presence/absence 0/1 per feature Gaussian NB Continuous features A normal distribution Two practical notes that come up: Laplace (add-one) smoothing is essential — without it, a single unseen word gives p = 0 p = 0 p = 0 and zeroes out the whole product. And NB probabilities are poorly calibrated (pushed toward 0 or 1 by the independence assumption), so trust its ranking and labels, not its confidence numbers. Memory hook Naive Bayes assumes every feature votes independently. The assumption is a lie, but the winner of the vote is usually still right — good classification, bad probabilities. Interview angle Why does Naive Bayes work if the independence assumption is false? The crisp answer: it only needs the right class to win the argmax, not calibrated probabilities; the errors are often shared across classes and cancel at the decision. Bonus points for mentioning Laplace smoothing and that it s a strong, near-free baseline for text. # k-NN and SVM — Distance vs Margin These two are usually taught together because they represent two opposite instincts about what makes a good boundary: be like your neighbors versus stay as far from everyone as possible . k-Nearest Neighbors is the laziest model there is — it does no training, just stores the data. To classify a point, it finds the k k k closest stored examples and takes a majority vote. Small k k k means a jagged, low-bias/high-variance boundary; large k k k smooths it out (higher bias, lower variance). Its weaknesses are exactly its design: prediction is slow (you compare against everything), it s memory-heavy, and it dies in high dimensions because distances become meaningless — the curse of dimensionality . It also demands feature scaling, since raw-scale features dominate the distance. Support Vector Machines take the opposite stance: among all lines that separate the classes, pick the one with the widest margin — the largest gap to the nearest points (the support vectors ). A wide margin is a built-in regularizer, which is why SVMs are strong in high-dimensional spaces like text. The kernel trick lets them draw nonlinear boundaries by implicitly mapping data to a higher-dimensional space without ever computing the coordinates — the RBF kernel is the common default. k-NN SVM Training None (lazy) Solve a convex optimization Idea Vote of nearest neighbors Maximize the margin Boundary Flexible, local Linear, or kernel for nonlinear Scales to big data? Predict is slow Training slow, predict fast Key knobs k k k , distance metric, scaling C C C (margin softness), kernel Memory hook k-NN: tell me who your neighbors are. SVM: draw the boundary down the widest empty street. One is lazy and local; the other is a global optimizer obsessed with the margin. Interview angle For k-NN expect what happens as k k k grows? (bias up, variance down) and why does it fail in high dimensions? (distances concentrate, neighbors stop being meaningful). For SVM expect what s a support vector? (a point on or inside the margin that defines the boundary) and what does the kernel trick buy you? (nonlinear boundaries without explicit high-dimensional features). Go deeper (optional) The SVM C C C parameter is the margin-softness knob: small C C C = wide, soft margin tolerating misclassifications (more bias, less variance); large C C C = narrow, hard margin fitting the training data tightly (less bias, more variance). It s the same bias-variance dial in margin clothing. # Trees, Forests, Boosting — Bagging vs Boosting Tree-based models dominate tabular data, and the progression from a single tree to forests to boosting is one of the most testable arcs in ML. A decision tree splits the feature space with a sequence of yes/no questions, choosing each split to most reduce impurity ( Gini or entropy for classification). It s wonderfully interpretable and handles mixed feature types with no scaling — but a single deep tree overfits badly and is unstable : change a few points and the whole tree can rearrange. That instability is the opening for ensembles. The two ways to combine many trees are the central contrast of this section. Bagging (Random Forest) Boosting (GBM / XGBoost) Trees are trained In parallel, independently Sequentially, each fixing the last Each tree sees A bootstrap sample (+ random feature subset at each split) The residual errors so far Primarily reduces Variance Bias Failure mode Slightly weaker than tuned boosting Overfits if over-trained / under-regularized Tuning burden Low (strong out of the box) Higher (learning rate, depth, rounds) Random forests grow many deep, decorrelated trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets, then average them. Averaging many high-variance, low-bias trees cancels the variance — a robust, low-maintenance default. Gradient boosting instead builds shallow trees one at a time, each trained on the previous ensemble s errors, steadily driving down bias. Tuned well (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), boosting is usually the top performer on heterogeneous tabular data. Memory hook Bagging = a committee voting in parallel to cancel each other s mistakes (kills variance). Boosting = a relay team , each runner covering the last one s shortfall (kills bias). Interview angle The bagging-vs-boosting contrast is asked constantly. Nail the one-liner: bagging trains independent trees in parallel to reduce variance; boosting trains dependent trees sequentially on residuals to reduce bias. Follow-ups: why are random-forest trees deep but boosting trees shallow? (deep = low-bias high-variance, perfect for averaging; shallow = weak learners boosting corrects gradually) and which overfits more easily? (boosting, since it keeps fitting residuals). # Ensembles in Full Zooming out, the ensembles above are three instances of one principle: combine many models so their errors cancel. Worth knowing all the named patterns. Method How it combines Mainly helps Bagging Parallel models on bootstrap samples, then average/vote Variance Boosting Sequential models on residuals Bias Stacking A meta-model learns to blend base models predictions Both (if base models are diverse) Voting Hard (majority) or soft (average probabilities) Variance The condition for an ensemble to help is diversity : the base models must make different errors. Averaging ten copies of the same model gains nothing. This is why random forests inject randomness (bootstrap rows + random feature subsets) — to decorrelate the trees so their mistakes don t line up. Memory hook An ensemble only helps if its members are wrong in different ways . Diversity is the whole trick — identical experts add nothing; disagreeing experts cancel each other s blind spots. Go deeper (optional) Stacking/blending of diverse models wins many Kaggle competitions: train diverse base models (trees, linear, nets), then a meta-learner on their out-of-fold predictions. The subtlety is leakage — the meta-model must be trained on held-out base predictions, or it learns from data the base models already saw. # Which Classifier When The payoff of the chapter: matching a model to the data in front of you. This is the decision interviewers actually want to see you make. Situation Reach for Need a fast, interpretable baseline Logistic regression Text / very high-dimensional sparse data Naive Bayes or linear SVM Tabular data, want top accuracy Gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) Tabular data, want robust + low tuning Random forest Images, audio, language Neural network Small data, low dimensions, nonlinear k-NN or SVM (RBF) Need calibrated probabilities Logistic regression (usually well calibrated), or calibrate afterward Need to explain every prediction Single decision tree or logistic regression The meta-strategy: always start with a simple baseline (logistic regression or a shallow tree), measure it honestly, then escalate to a stronger model only if the baseline leaves accuracy on the table. The baseline also catches leakage — a too-good baseline score is a red flag, not a victory. Interview angle You have a tabular dataset with 50k rows and mixed feature types — what do you use? Strong answer: a logistic-regression baseline for a reference point and calibration, then gradient-boosted trees as the likely winner, justified by their fit to heterogeneous tabular data and their handling of nonlinearities and interactions without manual feature engineering. Then mention you d validate the choice empirically — No Free Lunch. # Cross-Cutting Skills (Asked of Senior Candidates) Beyond naming models, senior interviews probe a few skills that cut across all classifiers. Handling class imbalance. When one class is rare (fraud, disease), accuracy is useless and most classifiers drift toward the majority. Levers: resample (SMOTE / oversample minority, undersample majority), reweight the loss to penalize minority errors more, and — most importantly — change the metric to precision/recall, F1, or PR-AUC instead of accuracy. Multiclass from binary models. Models like SVM are natively binary. One-vs-Rest trains one classifier per class against all others ( k k k classifiers); One-vs-One trains one per pair ( k ( k − 1 ) / 2 k(k-1)/2 k ( k − 1 ) /2 classifiers, each on less data). Logistic regression and trees handle multiclass natively via softmax / multi-way splits. Calibration. A model can rank well but report dishonest probabilities (Naive Bayes, SVMs, deep nets often do). If you need the number 0.7 to mean 70% of the time, calibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data (see Model Evaluation Validation ). Memory hook Three senior reflexes: imbalanced data → change the metric first, resampling/reweighting second. Binary-only model → wrap it in One-vs-Rest. Probabilities you ll act on → calibrate them. Rapid fire — Classification Two families: discriminative learns the boundary p ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) ; generative learns p ( x , y ) p(x,y) p ( x , y ) and can sample. Generative wins small-data, discriminative wins large-data. Logistic regression: linear in log-odds, sigmoid out, trained with convex cross-entropy. The boundary is linear; use it as the baseline. Naive Bayes: assumes conditional independence (false) but wins the argmax anyway; great for text; use Laplace smoothing; poorly calibrated. k-NN: lazy, local, dies in high dimensions, needs scaling. SVM: max-margin, strong in high-dim, kernel trick for nonlinearity. Trees overfit and are unstable. Bagging (random forest) = parallel trees killing variance; boosting (XGBoost) = sequential trees killing bias. Ensembles need diverse base models (wrong in different ways) to help. Pick by data: logistic baseline → boosting for tabular, NN for perceptual, NB/linear-SVM for text. Imbalance → change the metric (PR-AUC, F1) before resampling/reweighting. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember Two families Discriminative draws the boundary p ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) ; generative models p ( x , y ) p(x,y) p ( x , y ) and can sample. Logistic regression Linear in log-odds, sigmoid out, convex cross-entropy loss; the usually well-calibrated baseline. Why not MSE Cross-entropy is convex with non-vanishing gradients; it s the Bernoulli MLE. Naive Bayes Conditional-independence assumption is false but the argmax still wins; great, fast text baseline. k-NN Lazy, local, needs scaling, dies in high dimensions; k k k trades bias for variance. SVM Maximize the margin; kernel trick for nonlinear boundaries; strong in high dimensions. Trees Interpretable but overfit and unstable — the reason ensembles exist. Bagging vs boosting Bagging = parallel trees, kills variance (random forest). Boosting = sequential trees on residuals, kills bias (XGBoost). Ensembles Only help when base models are wrong in different ways — diversity is the trick. Which when Logistic baseline → boosting for tabular, NN for perceptual, NB/linear-SVM for text. Imbalance Change the metric first (PR-AUC, F1), then resample/reweight. # Related Logistic Regression Generative vs Discriminative Bagging vs Boosting Precision Recall Regression Methods

title: Generative vs Discriminative
text: Say it in 30s: Discriminative models learn the boundary directly — P(y | x) — they only answer which class. Generative models learn each class s shape — P(x | y) and P(y) — then use Bayes rule to derive P(y | x), so they can also generate new x. The canonical pair Logistic Regression (discriminative) vs Naive Bayes (generative). Discriminative usually wins with ample data (optimizes the thing you care about). Generative wins with little data or when you need to sample, detect outliers, or handle missing features. Examples Discriminative: logistic regression, SVMs, most neural net classifiers, random forests. Generative: Naive Bayes, GMMs, HMMs, and modern generative models (VAEs, diffusion, LLMs). Trap: generative in the classic sense (models P(x,y)) is a superset idea that also covers today s generative AI — be ready to bridge both meanings. See depth: Classification Methods (§2), Fundamentals (§1). Related: Logistic Regression , Maximum Likelihood Estimation .

title: Logistic Regression
text: Say it in 30s: A linear classifier that outputs a probability. It puts a linear combination of features through a sigmoid to get P(y=1), and is trained by minimizing cross-entropy (= maximum likelihood under a Bernoulli model). Despite the name, it s classification. Why it s the must-know baseline Outputs probabilities (usually reasonably well calibrated, unless heavily regularized, reweighted/resampled or misspecified), not just labels. Interpretable : a weight is the change in log-odds per unit feature; exp(weight) is an odds ratio. Convex loss → any local optimum is global (unique if strictly convex, i.e. full-rank X or L2-regularized), fast to train. The discriminative counterpart to Naive Bayes. Key points Decision boundary is linear; use feature engineering or kernels for nonlinearity. Regularize with L1 (sparse) or L2 (stable) — same penalties as linear regression. Multiclass via softmax (a.k.a. multinomial logistic regression). Trap: it can t separate XOR-like data without nonlinear features. Underfits genuinely nonlinear boundaries. See depth: Classification Methods (§3), TensorGym Study Notes . Related: Cross-Entropy Loss , Generative vs Discriminative , Gradient Descent , Precision Recall .

title: Support Vector Machines
text: Say it in 30s: An SVM finds the decision boundary that separates the classes with the widest possible margin — the hyperplane as far as possible from the nearest points of each class. Those nearest points are the support vectors and are the only ones that define the boundary. The kernel trick lets it draw nonlinear boundaries by computing dot products in a higher-dimensional space without ever building that space. Key points Boundary is a hyperplane w·x + b = 0 ; classify with sign(w·x + b) , labels coded y ∈ {+1, −1} . Fix the scale so on-margin support vectors satisfy y(w·x + b) = 1 (in the soft margin, violators have y(w·x + b) 1 ); then the half-margin is 1/||w|| , full margin 2/||w|| . Hard margin: minimize ½||w||² s.t. yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 . Minimizing ||w|| = maximizing the margin. Soft margin (real data): minimize ½||w||² + C·Σξᵢ s.t. yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 − ξᵢ , ξᵢ ≥ 0 . Slack ξ allows violations. C is the bias-variance knob: large C → punish violations hard (narrow margin, overfit risk); small C → tolerate violations (wider margin, more regularized). Kernel trick: the dual depends on the data only through dot products xᵢ·xⱼ , so replace them with a kernel K(xᵢ, xⱼ) to get a nonlinear boundary cheaply. Common kernels: RBF (Gaussian), polynomial, linear. Common follow-ups / traps What s the margin? → distance from the boundary to the nearest points ( 1/||w|| ; full margin width 2/||w|| ); SVM maximizes it. Which points matter? → only the support vectors; far-away points don t move the boundary. Why does the kernel trick work? → optimization needs only pairwise dot products, never the explicit high-dimensional features. What does C do? → trades margin width against training violations; it s the regularization parameter. Don t say SVM just draws a boundary — the defining idea is the maximum-margin boundary. See depth: Classification Methods . Related: Logistic Regression , Regularization , Bias-Variance Tradeoff .

title: Gated Recurrent Unit
text: A GRU is a streamlined LSTM : same core trick (gated, mostly-additive memory so gradients survive), but with one memory line instead of two and two gates instead of three. Fewer parameters → trains faster, needs less data, often just as good. # The setup No separate cell state — just one memory vector h h h — and two sigmoid gates. # The two gates Update gate ( σ \sigma σ ) — the main one. A single slider doing the forget and input jobs together: toward 1 = keep old memory, ignore new; toward 0 = drop old memory, take in new. Keeping is the opposite of adding (if you keep 70%, you take 30% new). Holding it near 1 across steps is what preserves long-range memory and the gradient. Reset gate ( σ \sigma σ ) — decides how much of the past to ignore when drafting the new candidate memory. Lets the cell start fresh when the current input begins something new and old context would be noise. One step in words: reset gate decides how much past to fold into a candidate new memory → update gate decides how much of that candidate to swap in versus how much old memory to keep. # Forward math (defined bottom-up) Symbols: σ \sigma σ squashes to ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) ( 0 , 1 ) (a dial), tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh to ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1,1) ( − 1 , 1 ) (signed content), ⊙ \odot ⊙ = elementwise multiply, [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] = concatenation, each W W W = a learned matrix. h h h is the single memory state. Define the two dials and the candidate first — each reads [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] : Update dial z t = σ ( W z [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) z_t = \sigma(W_z[h_{t-1},x_t]) z t ​ = σ ( W z ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much old memory to keep Reset dial r t = σ ( W r [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) r_t = \sigma(W_r[h_{t-1},x_t]) r t ​ = σ ( W r ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much past to use when drafting Candidate h ~ t = tanh ⁡ ( W h [ r t ⊙ h t − 1 , x t ] ) \tilde h_t = \tanh\big(W_h[\,r_t \odot h_{t-1},\, x_t\,]\big) h ~ t ​ = tanh ( W h ​ [ r t ​ ⊙ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] ) — note the past is filtered by r t r_t r t ​ before drafting Then blend old memory and candidate with the single update dial: h t = z t ⊙ h t − 1 + ( 1 − z t ) ⊙ h ~ t h_t = z_t \odot h_{t-1} + (1 - z_t)\odot \tilde h_t h t ​ = z t ​ ⊙ h t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − z t ​ ) ⊙ h ~ t ​ (PyTorch convention: z z z near 1 keeps the old memory.) Gradient: the leading term is ∂ h t ∂ h t − 1 ≈ diag ⁡ ( z t ) \dfrac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}} \approx \operatorname{diag}(z_t) ∂ h t − 1 ​ ∂ h t ​ ​ ≈ diag ( z t ​ ) , so holding z t ≈ 1 z_t \approx 1 z t ​ ≈ 1 keeps the gradient highway open — same additive trick as the LSTM, with one dial instead of separate forget/input gates. # Inside one GRU cell Inputs x t x_t x t ​ and h t − 1 h_{t-1} h t − 1 ​ feed both gates and the candidate. The reset gate filters the past before the candidate is drafted; the update gate blends candidate vs. old memory at the very end. Convention here matches the note and PyTorch: z near 1 keeps the old memory , so the candidate h ~ \tilde h h ~ gets weight ( 1 − z ) (1-z) ( 1 − z ) . Some textbooks flip this; the math is identical, only the label on the dial moves. (Caveat: the candidate above is the original Cho form tanh ⁡ ( W [ r ⊙ h , x ] ) \tanh(W[r\odot h, x]) tanh ( W [ r ⊙ h , x ]) ; PyTorch applies the reset gate after the hidden matmul: n = tanh ⁡ ( W i n x + b i n + r ⊙ ( W h n h + b h n ) ) n=\tanh(W_{in}x+b_{in}+r\odot(W_{hn}h+b_{hn})) n = tanh ( W in ​ x + b in ​ + r ⊙ ( W hn ​ h + b hn ​ )) .) # The step, as a sequence # Stacking GRUs Real models rarely use one layer. You stack them: the hidden-state sequence from layer 1 becomes the input sequence to layer 2, and so on. Two directions of information flow, and they don t mix: Sideways (through time): each layer keeps its own hidden state h h h and passes it to its future self at the next timestep. Layer 1 and layer 2 each have a separate memory line. Upward (through depth): at each timestep, a layer s output is fed as the input to the layer above it. Lower layers tend to pick up short, local patterns; higher layers compose them into longer-range structure. Only the top layer s outputs are usually read for predictions. More layers add representational depth but cost compute and can overfit on small data — same tradeoff as stacking anything. num_layers in PyTorch s nn.GRU does exactly this stacking for you. # LSTM vs GRU LSTM GRU Memories 2 (cell + hidden) 1 (merged) Gates 3 (forget, input, output) 2 (update, reset) Params more fewer Strength slight edge on very long / complex sequences faster, leaner, less data Neither changes the loss ( cross-entropy ). In practice: try both, pick by validation. GRU is a sensible default for speed or limited data; LSTM when sequences are long and complex. # 30-second answer A GRU merges the LSTM s two memories into one and uses two gates: an update gate (keep-old vs take-new in a single dial) and a reset gate (how much past to use when forming the candidate). Same gradient-saving idea as the LSTM, with less machinery. # See also Long Short-Term Memory — the fuller version Recurrent Neural Networks — the base cell both upgrade Cross-Entropy Loss · Gradient Descent

title: Graph Neural Networks
text: A GNN learns from data that lives on a graph — entities (nodes) wired together by relations (edges) — instead of a grid (images, CNNs ) or a sequence (text, RNNs ). The core trick is message passing : each node repeatedly updates its own vector by mixing in its neighbors vectors. Stack k k k rounds and a node sees everything within k k k hops. # The setup A graph is nodes plus edges. Every node v v v starts with a feature vector x v x_v x v ​ (its raw attributes). The model learns from the features and the wiring — that s the whole reason to reach for a graph model rather than a plain MLP over the features alone. Three things a GNN can predict, depending on where you read out: node level — a label per node (fraud user, spam page) edge level — does a link exist / what kind (recommendation, knowledge graph) graph level — one label for the whole graph (molecule property) # Message passing — the engine Let h v ( k ) h_v^{(k)} h v ( k ) ​ be node v v v s vector after layer k k k , with h v ( 0 ) = x v h_v^{(0)} = x_v h v ( 0 ) ​ = x v ​ . One layer is three functions: Message — for each neighbor u u u , build a message m u → v = MSG ( h u , h v , e u v ) m_{u\to v} = \text{MSG}(h_u, h_v, e_{uv}) m u → v ​ = MSG ( h u ​ , h v ​ , e uv ​ ) , where e u v e_{uv} e uv ​ is an optional edge feature. Aggregate — collapse all neighbor messages into one vector with a permutation-invariant operator (sum, mean, or max — the result can t depend on neighbor order): a v = AGG ( { m u → v : u ∈ N ( v ) } ) a_v = \text{AGG}(\{m_{u\to v} : u \in \mathcal N(v)\}) a v ​ = AGG ({ m u → v ​ : u ∈ N ( v )}) . Update — fold the aggregate back into the node: h v ( k ) = UPDATE ( h v ( k − 1 ) , a v ) h_v^{(k)} = \text{UPDATE}(h_v^{(k-1)}, a_v) h v ( k ) ​ = UPDATE ( h v ( k − 1 ) ​ , a v ​ ) . Every architecture below is just a different choice of these three functions. # GCN — the equation worth memorizing H ( k ) = σ ( D ~ − 1 / 2 A ~ D ~ − 1 / 2 H ( k − 1 ) W ( k ) ) H^{(k)} = \sigma\big(\tilde D^{-1/2}\,\tilde A\,\tilde D^{-1/2}\,H^{(k-1)}\,W^{(k)}\big) H ( k ) = σ ( D ~ − 1/2 A ~ D ~ − 1/2 H ( k − 1 ) W ( k ) ) A ~ = A + I \tilde A = A + I A ~ = A + I — adjacency with self-loops (so a node includes itself). D ~ \tilde D D ~ — diagonal degree matrix of A ~ \tilde A A ~ . W ( k ) W^{(k)} W ( k ) — the only learned parameter in the layer; σ \sigma σ — a nonlinearity (ReLU). Per node: h v ( k ) = σ ⁣ ( ∑ u ∈ N ( v ) ∪ { v } 1 d ~ v d ~ u W ( k ) h u ( k − 1 ) ) h_v^{(k)} = \sigma\!\Bigg(\sum_{u \in \mathcal N(v)\cup\{v\}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde d_v\,\tilde d_u}}\, W^{(k)} h_u^{(k-1)}\Bigg) h v ( k ) ​ = σ ( u ∈ N ( v ) ∪ { v } ∑ ​ d ~ v ​ d ~ u ​ ​ 1 ​ W ( k ) h u ( k − 1 ) ​ ) So GCN s message weight is pure geometry ( 1 / d ~ v d ~ u 1/\sqrt{\tilde d_v\tilde d_u} 1/ d ~ v ​ d ~ u ​ ​ ) — no learned per-edge importance, which is its main weakness. The symmetric normalization down-weights high-degree hub neighbors and keeps the operator s eigenvalues real and bounded (which both stabilizes training and, as below, causes oversmoothing). # GAT — learn the weights Replace the fixed coefficient with a learned attention weight α v u \alpha_{vu} α v u ​ : h v ( k ) = σ ⁣ ( ∑ u α v u W h u ( k − 1 ) ) , α v u = exp ⁡ ( e v u ) ∑ w exp ⁡ ( e v w ) , e v u = LeakyReLU ( a ⊤ [ W h v ∥ W h u ] ) h_v^{(k)} = \sigma\!\Bigg(\sum_{u} \alpha_{vu}\, W h_u^{(k-1)}\Bigg), \qquad \alpha_{vu} = \frac{\exp(e_{vu})}{\sum_{w} \exp(e_{vw})}, \quad e_{vu} = \text{LeakyReLU}\big(a^\top[Wh_v \,\Vert\, Wh_u]\big) h v ( k ) ​ = σ ( u ∑ ​ α v u ​ W h u ( k − 1 ) ​ ) , α v u ​ = ∑ w ​ exp ( e v w ​ ) exp ( e v u ​ ) ​ , e v u ​ = LeakyReLU ( a ⊤ [ W h v ​ ∥ W h u ​ ] ) Now the weight depends on the content of the two nodes, not just structure. Essentially a transformer -style attention where the adjacency matrix is the attention mask. Usually multi-head. # GraphSAGE — the scalable template h v ( k ) = σ ( W ⋅ [ h v ( k − 1 ) ∥ AGG ( { h u ( k − 1 ) } ) ] ) h_v^{(k)} = \sigma\Big(W \cdot \big[\,h_v^{(k-1)} \,\Vert\, \text{AGG}(\{h_u^{(k-1)}\})\,\big]\Big) h v ( k ) ​ = σ ( W ⋅ [ h v ( k − 1 ) ​ ∥ AGG ({ h u ( k − 1 ) ​ }) ] ) It concatenates self with the neighbor aggregate (keeps node identity), and samples a fixed number of neighbors instead of using all — that s what makes it run on billion-edge graphs and work inductively on unseen nodes. # GIN — maximally expressive h v ( k ) = MLP ( k ) ⁣ ( ( 1 + ϵ ) h v ( k − 1 ) + ∑ u ∈ N ( v ) h u ( k − 1 ) ) h_v^{(k)} = \text{MLP}^{(k)}\!\Big((1+\epsilon)\,h_v^{(k-1)} + \sum_{u\in\mathcal N(v)} h_u^{(k-1)}\Big) h v ( k ) ​ = MLP ( k ) ( ( 1 + ϵ ) h v ( k − 1 ) ​ + u ∈ N ( v ) ∑ ​ h u ( k − 1 ) ​ ) Uses sum , not mean or max, on purpose: mean can t tell { A , B } \{A,B\} { A , B } from { A , A , B , B } \{A,A,B,B\} { A , A , B , B } , max can t tell { A , B } \{A,B\} { A , B } from { A , A , B } \{A,A,B\} { A , A , B } . Only sum is injective over a multiset (preserves counts). This is the link to the Weisfeiler-Lehman test — GIN hits the 1-WL expressiveness ceiling. Sum is needed to reach the 1-WL ceiling; mean or max fall below it. # The three side by side A spectrum: structure decides everything (GCN) → content decides (GAT) → preserve maximum structural info (GIN). Cost: GCN ≈ GIN GAT; expressiveness order is GCN GAT/GraphSAGE GIN (for structure). None dominates: GAT often wins on feature-rich graphs, GIN on molecules, GCN is a shockingly hard baseline for the compute. # Depth, outputs, and oversmoothing One layer = see direct neighbors; two layers = neighbors of neighbors. Depth = reach. Then pool the final embeddings into the right readout head. Oversmoothing (the reason GNNs stay shallow, 2–4 layers): strip weights/nonlinearity and a layer is repeated multiplication by A ^ = D ~ − 1 / 2 A ~ D ~ − 1 / 2 \hat A = \tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2} A ^ = D ~ − 1/2 A ~ D ~ − 1/2 , so k k k layers ≈ A ^ k H \approx \hat A^k H ≈ A ^ k H . The eigenvalues of A ^ \hat A A ^ live in ( − 1 , 1 ] (-1,1] ( − 1 , 1 ] with the leading one at exactly 1 1 1 , so every other component is shrunk by λ k → 0 \lambda^k \to 0 λ k → 0 . All node embeddings collapse toward the dominant eigenvector — they become indistinguishable. This is why just add layers (which works for CNNs/transformers) actively hurts here. Residual connections, normalization, and jumping-knowledge layers fight this. Oversquashing — a related failure: a node s exponentially growing receptive field gets crammed into a fixed-size vector, so long-range dependencies get lost. # Training: losses, activations, batching There is no special GNN loss . The GNN produces embeddings; a readout head turns them into predictions, and the loss follows the head and task level (see Cross-Entropy Loss ). Node / graph classification — cross-entropy (softmax + CE for multi-class, sigmoid + BCE for binary/multi-label). In the transductive setting, compute the loss only over labeled training nodes even though message passing uses the whole graph. Regression (molecule property, ETA) — MSE or MAE / Huber. Link prediction — the one with a GNN-specific flavor. Score a candidate edge ( u , v ) (u,v) ( u , v ) from the two embeddings (dot product h u ⊤ h v h_u^\top h_v h u ⊤ ​ h v ​ or an MLP on [ h u ∥ h v ] [h_u \Vert h_v] [ h u ​ ∥ h v ​ ] ), then train with negative sampling + BCE or a margin/ranking loss (BPR, max-margin). # Negative sampling Link prediction has ∼ N 2 \sim N^2 ∼ N 2 possible pairs but only a few million real edges, so almost everything is a non-edge . You can t compute the loss over all negatives (intractable + hopelessly imbalanced — predict no edge everywhere and score 99.9999%). Instead, for each positive edge sample a handful of negatives (typically 1:1 to 1:5 ), usually by fixing u u u and drawing a random w w w it isn t linked to. Train the scorer to output high for real edges, low for sampled fakes . Same trick appears in word2vec (avoids a full-vocab softmax), recommendations/retrieval, and contrastive learning. The detail interviewers probe: Hard negative mining — sample negatives the model currently scores high (plausible fakes) for a stronger gradient than uniform-random easy negatives. Frequency/degree-based sampling (word2vec used freq 0.75 ^{0.75} 0.75 ) to avoid over-sampling popular nodes. False-negative noise — a sampled negative may be a true-but-missing link; usually tolerated because it s rare. One-liner: negative sampling approximates an impossibly large negative set with a small representative (or deliberately hard) sample, turning all-vs-all into positive-vs-few-negatives. # Activations Nothing exotic. ReLU is the default σ \sigma σ between layers. LeakyReLU is a fixed architectural choice inside GAT s attention scoring ; ELU is a common GAT alternative. At the head: softmax (multi-class), sigmoid (binary / multi-label / link probability), linear (regression). The aggregator (sum/mean/max) is the pooling operator, not an activation, and must stay permutation-invariant. # The engineering gotchas Normalization — vanilla BatchNorm is awkward (batch = variable-size set of nodes/graphs); use LayerNorm , GraphNorm , or PairNorm (PairNorm is designed to fight oversmoothing ). Deeper GNNs = normalization + residuals + jumping-knowledge. Self-loops — A ~ = A + I \tilde A = A + I A ~ = A + I so a node keeps its own features in the aggregation. Pooling for graph-level tasks — sum vs mean has the same expressiveness tradeoff as AGG (sum keeps size/count, mean normalizes it away); GIN recommends sum. Mini-batching is not row-slicing — either neighbor sampling (GraphSAGE) or subgraph batching (Cluster-GCN, GraphSAINT) for graphs too big for memory. Edge features — plain GCN/GAT use node features only; thread e u v e_{uv} e uv ​ through the message function (general MPNN ), or use R-GCN for typed edges in knowledge graphs (one weight matrix per relation). Optimizer — just Adam, nothing GNN-specific. # Use cases production Recommendations — Pinterest PinSage (GraphSAGE on the pin–board graph) is the classic deployed example; Uber Eats, Alibaba similar. Fraud / abuse — fraud rings are graph structure; isolated features miss them. Payments, marketplaces. Molecules / drug discovery — graph-level property prediction on molecular graphs. Maps / logistics — Google used a GNN for ETA prediction over the road graph. Knowledge graphs — link prediction, entity resolution (R-GCN handles typed edges). # Where they fail Oversmoothing / oversquashing — limits depth and long-range reach (above). Scalability — neighbor explosion: a k k k -hop neighborhood can be most of the graph. Sampling helps but adds variance. Dynamic graphs — most GNNs assume a static graph; real graphs change constantly, and serving fresh embeddings is a real eng problem. Often don t beat simpler baselines — a tuned MLP + hand-engineered graph features frequently matches published GNN wins. If the signal is in node features, not topology, a GNN is overkill. Always benchmark a non-graph baseline first. # Metrics Depends on the task level (see Precision Recall , ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC ): Node / graph classification — accuracy, F1, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR (use PR for fraud — heavy class imbalance). Link prediction — AUC plus ranking metrics: Hits@k, MRR (mean reciprocal rank), MAP. Recommendation — Recall@k, NDCG@k, MRR. Regression (molecules, ETA) — MAE, RMSE. # One-line recall A GNN layer only chooses how to weight a neighbor (MSG), how to combine weighted neighbors (AGG), and how to fold that into the node (UPDATE). GCN fixes weights by degree, GAT learns them by content, GraphSAGE samples + concatenates, GIN sums and proves that s maximal. Everything else is plumbing. # See also Convolutional Neural Networks — convolution on a grid; GNN generalizes it to arbitrary graphs Recurrent Neural Networks — attention link to GAT Gradient Descent — how the weights W W W are trained ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC · Precision Recall — the classification metrics above Cross-Entropy Loss — the usual node/graph classification loss Home

title: Long Short-Term Memory
text: An LSTM is an RNN cell that fixes vanishing gradients by adding a second memory line — the cell state — that information rides along with only gentle edits (keep + add) instead of being fully overwritten every step. Learned gates (sigmoid dials, 0→1) decide what to erase, what to write, and what to read. The name says it: it makes short-term memory able to act long-term. # The two memories Cell state c c c — the long-term memory. A conveyor belt running across all steps. It mostly gets multiplied (forget) and added to (input), never fully rewritten. That additive path is why information and gradients survive long gaps. Hidden state h h h — the short-term memory / working output. What the cell exposes right now to predict and pass forward. A vanilla RNN has only h h h (hence it forgets). The LSTM s innovation is the added c c c line. # What a gate is A gate is a tiny layer that outputs a number between 0 and 1 via sigmoid — a dial. 0 = block, 1 = let through. You multiply the dial against some information. The network learns to set the dial from context (it sees the new input x t x_t x t ​ and previous output h t − 1 h_{t-1} h t − 1 ​ ). # The three gates Forget gate ( σ \sigma σ ) — multiplies the belt to decide what to erase . Near 1 = keep the memory; near 0 = wipe it. (New subject in the sentence → drop the old one.) Input gate ( σ \sigma σ paired with a tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh candidate) — decides what new content to add to the belt. The tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh proposes candidate content; the sigmoid decides how much of it to write. Output gate ( σ \sigma σ ) — decides how much of the belt to read out as the hidden state h t h_t h t ​ . One step in words: look at x t x_t x t ​ and h t − 1 h_{t-1} h t − 1 ​ → forget some of the belt → add new content to the belt → read a filtered view as the output. # Forward math (defined bottom-up) Symbols: σ \sigma σ squashes to ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) ( 0 , 1 ) (a dial), tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh to ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1,1) ( − 1 , 1 ) (signed content), ⊙ \odot ⊙ = elementwise multiply, [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] = concatenation, each W W W = a learned matrix. c c c = cell-state belt, h h h = hidden state. Define the four pieces first — each just reads [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] : Forget dial f t = σ ( W f [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) f_t = \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1},x_t]) f t ​ = σ ( W f ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much of the old belt to keep Input dial i t = σ ( W i [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) i_t = \sigma(W_i[h_{t-1},x_t]) i t ​ = σ ( W i ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much new content to write Candidate g t = tanh ⁡ ( W g [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) g_t = \tanh(W_g[h_{t-1},x_t]) g t ​ = tanh ( W g ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — the proposed new content (signed → tanh) Output dial o t = σ ( W o [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) o_t = \sigma(W_o[h_{t-1},x_t]) o t ​ = σ ( W o ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much of the belt to expose Then assemble — update the belt (keep some old, add some new), then read it out: c t = f t ⊙ c t − 1 + i t ⊙ g t c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t c t ​ = f t ​ ⊙ c t − 1 ​ + i t ​ ⊙ g t ​ h t = o t ⊙ tanh ⁡ ( c t ) h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) h t ​ = o t ​ ⊙ tanh ( c t ​ ) Gradient highway: because the belt update is additive , ∂ c t ∂ c t − 1 ≈ diag ⁡ ( f t ) \dfrac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} \approx \operatorname{diag}(f_t) ∂ c t − 1 ​ ∂ c t ​ ​ ≈ diag ( f t ​ ) — just the forget gate, not a tanh ⁡ ′ W \tanh W tanh ′ W matrix. Chained across time it s ∏ i diag ⁡ ( f i ) \prod_i \operatorname{diag}(f_i) ∏ i ​ diag ( f i ​ ) ; if the net learns f i ≈ 1 f_i \approx 1 f i ​ ≈ 1 the gradient survives undimmed (the constant error carousel ). # Why it fixes vanishing gradients In a plain RNN the backward chain multiplied tanh ⁡ ′ ⋅ W \tanh \cdot W tanh ′ ⋅ W at every hop and collapsed to ~0. In an LSTM the cell-state s backward term is roughly just the forget-gate value . If the network learns to hold that gate near 1, the gradient flows back across many steps almost undimmed. The gates create a near-multiplication-free highway for the gradient. # Stacking layers Stack LSTMs by feeding one layer s hidden-state sequence as the input sequence to the layer above. The wrinkle vs. a plain RNN stack: each layer carries two lines sideways through time — the cell state c c c and the hidden state h h h — but only h h h is passed upward to the next layer. The c c c belt is private to its layer and never leaves it. So depth and time stay orthogonal: c c c and h h h flow left-to-right within a layer; only h h h flows bottom-to-top across layers. Top layer s h h h is read for predictions. num_layers in PyTorch s nn.LSTM builds this for you. # 30-second answer An LSTM adds a long-term cell-state belt alongside the short-term hidden state, and three sigmoid gates (forget = erase, input = write, output = read). The belt carries memory by keep-and-add rather than overwrite, so both information and gradients survive long sequences. It does not change the loss ( cross-entropy stays the same) — only the memory-update machinery. # See also Recurrent Neural Networks — the base cell LSTM upgrades Gated Recurrent Unit — the leaner cousin (1 memory, 2 gates) Cross-Entropy Loss · Gradient Descent

Backprop  weight update — order and timing (deep dive)
Is the update layer-by-layer or all at once?
Does layer 's update account for layer 's update?
text: ML + PyTorch study notes: weights, activations, and how backprop actually updates a network. # Weight initialization Initial weights are random and small (bias often 0, though nn.Linear draws it randomly too). Random, not zero — if all weights start equal, every neuron computes the same thing and gets the same update forever (the symmetry problem ). Randomness lets neurons specialize. Small, not huge — too big → signal/gradients explode (NaN); too small → they vanish (learns slowly). Principled inits scale randomness by layer fan: Xavier/Glorot (fan_in + fan_out; sigmoid/tanh) or He/Kaiming (fan_in; ReLU). nn.Linear uses a Kaiming-uniform variant by default (≈U(±1/√fan_in), bias also random); call nn.init.xavier_* or kaiming_* explicitly for tanh or ReLU. Set torch.manual_seed(42) for reproducible runs. # Weights bias are linear; activations are nonlinear A neuron has two parts: z = X W + b (linear: weights = slope, bias = intercept) a = activation ( z ) (nonlinear) z = XW + b \quad \text{(linear: weights = slope, bias = intercept)} \qquad a = \text{activation}(z) \quad \text{(nonlinear)} z = X W + b (linear: weights = slope, bias = intercept) a = activation ( z ) (nonlinear) Weights and bias do plain linear math ( y = m x + c y = mx + c y = m x + c ). Both are learned, both updated by gradient descent. The activation function is what s nonlinear (and it s fixed, not learned). Why needed: stacking linear layers with no activation collapses to one linear equation. Activations let the network model curves/complex patterns. Mental model: linear step → bend → linear step → bend → … # How weights are updated (gradient descent) One formula: w new = w old − ( η × gradient ) w_{\text{new}} = w_{\text{old}} - (\eta \times \text{gradient}) w new ​ = w old ​ − ( η × gradient ) Gradient = direction steepness of how loss changes with the weight. positive → increasing the weight raises loss → decrease it. negative → increasing the weight lowers loss → increase it. Either way you move opposite the gradient → hence the minus sign ( descent ). Learning rate η \eta η = step size. too big → overshoot, bounce around, diverge. too small → painfully slow. Hill analogy: gradient points steepest uphill; you step downhill (opposite) repeatedly until you reach the valley (low loss). Optimizers: plain SGD uses the formula directly; Adam adapts the step size per weight, but the core move opposite the gradient logic is the same. # How gradients are calculated (backpropagation) Backprop = the chain rule applied backwards through the network. In words: if A affects B and B affects C, then A s effect on C = = = (A→B) × \times × (B→C). Just multiply the links. # Worked single-neuron example Setup: x = [ 1 , 4 ] x = [1, 4] x = [ 1 , 4 ] , y = 0 y = 0 y = 0 , w = [ 0.5 , 0.5 ] w = [0.5, 0.5] w = [ 0.5 , 0.5 ] , b = 0 b = 0 b = 0 . z = 0.5 ⋅ 1 + 0.5 ⋅ 4 = 2.5 , p = σ ( 2.5 ) = 0.924 z = 0.5\cdot1 + 0.5\cdot4 = 2.5, \qquad p = \sigma(2.5) = 0.924 z = 0.5 ⋅ 1 + 0.5 ⋅ 4 = 2.5 , p = σ ( 2.5 ) = 0.924 Chain for w 1 w_1 w 1 ​ : w 1 → z → p → Loss \;w_1 \to z \to p \to \text{Loss} w 1 ​ → z → p → Loss . ∂ L ∂ w 1 = ∂ L ∂ p ⋅ ∂ p ∂ z ⋅ ∂ z ∂ w 1 = p − y p ( 1 − p ) ⋅ p ( 1 − p ) ⋅ x 1 = ( p − y ) x 1 \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial p}\cdot\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\cdot\frac{\partial z}{\partial w_1} = \frac{p-y}{p(1-p)}\cdot p(1-p)\cdot x_1 = (p - y)\,x_1 ∂ w 1 ​ ∂ L ​ = ∂ p ∂ L ​ ⋅ ∂ z ∂ p ​ ⋅ ∂ w 1 ​ ∂ z ​ = p ( 1 − p ) p − y ​ ⋅ p ( 1 − p ) ⋅ x 1 ​ = ( p − y ) x 1 ​ The p ( 1 − p ) p(1-p) p ( 1 − p ) cancels. Plugging in: ∂ L ∂ w 1 = ( 0.924 − 0 ) ⋅ 1 = 0.924 , ∂ L ∂ w 2 = ( 0.924 ) ⋅ 4 = 3.70 , ∂ L ∂ b = 0.924 \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = (0.924 - 0)\cdot 1 = 0.924, \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2} = (0.924)\cdot 4 = 3.70, \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = 0.924 ∂ w 1 ​ ∂ L ​ = ( 0.924 − 0 ) ⋅ 1 = 0.924 , ∂ w 2 ​ ∂ L ​ = ( 0.924 ) ⋅ 4 = 3.70 , ∂ b ∂ L ​ = 0.924 # Why the gradient is per-weight Every weight shares the same error term ( p − y ) (p - y) ( p − y ) but is multiplied by its own input x i x_i x i ​ . Different input → different gradient. ( w 2 w_2 w 2 ​ s input was 4, so its gradient is 4× w 1 w_1 w 1 ​ s.) # General per-weight formula gradient for a weight = ( error signal at its neuron ) × ( input flowing through it ) \text{gradient for a weight} = (\text{error signal at its neuron}) \times (\text{input flowing through it}) gradient for a weight = ( error signal at its neuron ) × ( input flowing through it ) Same error × input shape at every layer, however deep. # Multi-layer: why back For an earlier-layer weight the chain is longer (more links multiplied). The front part of that product is shared by all weights feeding a neuron, so backprop computes it once at the output and passes it backward as an error signal δ \delta δ . Working right-to-left avoids recomputing shared pieces — that s the efficiency trick. # Division of labor in PyTorch forward pass → compute prediction, autograd records every operation. loss.backward() → chain-rule backwards, store one gradient per weight in weight.grad . opt.step() → use the gradients to nudge every weight simultaneously. # Backprop weight update — order and timing (deep dive) # Is the update layer-by-layer or all at once? All at once, at the end. No weight changes during backprop. 1. forward pass - compute predictions using CURRENT weights 2. backward pass - compute the GRADIENT for every weight in every layer (last layer - first layer, but ONLY computing numbers) 3. opt.step() - NOW update every weight in every layer SIMULTANEOUSLY The weights are frozen during the entire forward + backward pass. Backprop going right-to-left is only about computing gradients efficiently, not about updating in stages. # Does layer t t t s update account for layer t + 1 t+1 t + 1 s update? No. Every gradient is computed w.r.t. the current (old) weights , assuming all other weights stay fixed. Each gradient answers: If I nudge this one weight a tiny bit and everything else stays put, how does the loss change? Then opt.step() nudges every weight at once — each under the assumption the others didn t move. # Doesn t that overcorrect? It can — and the learning rate is what keeps it safe. A gradient is only exactly true for an infinitesimally small step (it s a local linear approximation). The interaction between two layers updates is a higher-order effect: small × small = tiny 2 \text{small} \times \text{small} = \text{tiny}^2 small × small = tiny 2 → negligible when steps are small. weight change ≈ small , inter-layer interaction ≈ small × small = tiny 2 \text{weight change} \approx \text{small}, \qquad \text{inter-layer interaction} \approx \text{small} \times \text{small} = \text{tiny}^2 weight change ≈ small , inter-layer interaction ≈ small × small = tiny 2 So a small learning rate keeps the everyone else held fixed assumption valid. Any mismatch this round is re-measured and corrected next round. This is partly why too large a learning rate diverges : big steps make the layers interfere strongly, the assumption breaks, the overcorrection actually happens, and loss bounces/explodes. # Mental model One iteration = a single synchronized step where every layer moves as if the others didn t. Deliberately wrong but self-correcting: many small approximate steps, re-measuring all gradients each time, beats one big perfect jump. Over many iterations the whole network converges together. (Fancier optimizers, batch-norm, second-order methods exist partly to handle these inter-layer interactions better — plain gradient descent just relies on small steps + repeat. ) # Quick reference: the whole picture 1. Get data (pandas) - preprocess (fit on train only) - convert to tensors 2. Init weights randomly (small) 3. For each epoch: forward: guess = activation(X·W + b) loss: measure wrongness backward: chain-rule back - gradient per weight (error × input) step: new = old − lr × gradient (every weight at once) 4. Loss curve slides down = learning 5. Evaluate on validation (eval mode, no_grad) # Related Gradient Descent Cross-Entropy Loss Logistic Regression TensorGym Study Notes

title: Recurrent Neural Networks
text: An RNN reads a sequence one item at a time, keeping a memory (hidden state) that summarizes everything seen so far. It predicts the next item from that memory. The whole game: one cell, one set of weights, reused at every step , with the memory passed forward and rewritten each step. Its fatal flaw is forgetting — the trace of early items fades, so it can t learn long-range dependencies. LSTMs and GRUs fix exactly that. # The core computation (one step) At each step t t t the cell takes the new input x t x_t x t ​ and the previous memory h t − 1 h_{t-1} h t − 1 ​ , and produces the new memory: h t = tanh ⁡ ( W x h x t + W h h h t − 1 + b ) h_t = \tanh(W_{xh}\, x_t + W_{hh}\, h_{t-1} + b) h t ​ = tanh ( W x h ​ x t ​ + W hh ​ h t − 1 ​ + b ) y ^ t = softmax ( W h y h t ) \hat{y}_t = \text{softmax}(W_{hy}\, h_t) y ^ ​ t ​ = softmax ( W h y ​ h t ​ ) Read it as two streams meeting: the input s contribution ( W x h x t W_{xh} x_t W x h ​ x t ​ ) plus the memory s contribution ( W h h h t − 1 W_{hh} h_{t-1} W hh ​ h t − 1 ​ ), added together, then squashed by tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh into ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1, 1) ( − 1 , 1 ) . The squash is a pressure valve — it stops the memory from exploding over a long sequence and adds the non-linearity that makes the net expressive. There are a few distinct weight matrices, each with its own job: W x h W_{xh} W x h ​ — maps the input into memory space. W h h W_{hh} W hh ​ — maps old memory to new memory (the recurrence). W h y W_{hy} W h y ​ — maps memory to an output prediction. Notation key σ \sigma σ = sigmoid, squashes any number to ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) ( 0 , 1 ) (a dial ); tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh = squashes to ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1,1) ( − 1 , 1 ) (signed content). ⊙ \odot ⊙ = elementwise multiply (two vectors, slot by slot) — distinct from matrix-vector multiply like W h h h t − 1 W_{hh}h_{t-1} W hh ​ h t − 1 ​ . [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] = concatenation (glue the two vectors into one). Subscripts t , k , i t,k,i t , k , i are timestep indices. Caution: in tanh ⁡ ′ ( z i ) \tanh (z_i) tanh ′ ( z i ​ ) the z i z_i z i ​ is the pre-activation (the stuff inside the tanh), unrelated to the GRU update gate z t z_t z t ​ . # Weight sharing (the defining feature) The same W x h , W h h , W h y W_{xh}, W_{hh}, W_{hy} W x h ​ , W hh ​ , W h y ​ are reused at every time step. Same matrices across layers means across time — step 2 does not get fresh weights, it reuses step 1 s. Consequences: The model handles sequences of any length without adding parameters. It s one cell that loops , not a stack of distinct layers. The nodes in a drawing are the same cell at different times. # One evolving memory, not many There is one memory that takes a new value each step. h 1 , h 2 , h 3 h_1, h_2, h_3 h 1 ​ , h 2 ​ , h 3 ​ are not separate memories — they are snapshots of the same memory over time, like frames of a video. Each step reads the memory it was handed, computes a fresh updated version, and passes it forward . A node does not keep a private memory; the memory flows through each node, getting rewritten as it goes (note-passing down a row of people). # Stacking layers Don t confuse unrolling over time (the same one cell reused at each step) with stacking layers (genuinely different cells with their own weights, piled on top of each other). You can do both at once: stack layers, and unroll the whole stack over time. The hidden-state sequence from layer 1 becomes the input sequence to layer 2. Two flows that don t mix: each layer carries its own hidden state sideways through time, and at each timestep a layer s output feeds up as the next layer s input. Only the top layer s outputs are read for predictions. Note that stacking does not fix forgetting — without gates, each layer s sideways memory still fades, which is the whole reason LSTM / GRU exist. # Loss Next-item prediction uses cross-entropy , summed over the sequence: L = ∑ t = 1 T L t , L t = − log ⁡ y ^ t [ correct item ] L = \sum_{t=1}^{T} L_t, \qquad L_t = -\log \hat{y}_t[\text{correct item}] L = t = 1 ∑ T ​ L t ​ , L t ​ = − lo g y ^ ​ t ​ [ correct item ] The pipeline is softmax then cross-entropy : softmax ( p i = e z i / ∑ j e z j p_i = e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j} p i ​ = e z i ​ / ∑ j ​ e z j ​ ) turns raw scores into probabilities; cross-entropy ( − log ⁡ p correct -\log p_{\text{correct}} − lo g p correct ​ ) measures how little probability you gave the right answer. They are two consecutive operations, easy to conflate — the divide by the sum lives in softmax, the log lives in cross-entropy. # Training: Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) BPTT is ordinary backprop — applied to the RNN. The full cycle for one batch: Forward — run all steps, save h 1 … h T h_1 \dots h_T h 1 ​ … h T ​ , compute the loss. (memory changes here; weights frozen) Unroll — lay the loop out as a chain of repeated cells, one box per step, so it looks like a normal deep network. Backward — walk from the loss back through the chain, computing a gradient contribution at each step. (memory frozen; gradients computed here) Update — the optimizer ( SGD/Adam ) nudges the weights once , using the summed gradient. (weights change here) Unrolling = stretching the loop memory → [cell] → memory → [cell] → ... into a row [step1] → [step2] → [step3] so the chain rule applies like in any feedforward net. The one thing BPTT adds over plain backprop: because the weights are shared across steps, each step gives a gradient contribution for the same W W W , so you sum them across time , then update once. (You can t update mid-walk — step 3 s gradient assumed the old W W W .) Compute vs. update Gradients are computed at every node; the weights are updated only once, after summing all the per-step contributions. BPTT computes gradients, the optimizer spends them. # Why long-range learning fails (vanishing gradients) To send the gradient from a late step t t t back to an early step k k k , it must pass through every step in between, multiplying a Jacobian at each hop: ∂ h t ∂ h k = ∏ i = k + 1 t diag ⁡ ⁣ ( tanh ⁡ ′ ( z i ) ) W h h \frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_k} = \prod_{i=k+1}^{t} \operatorname{diag}\!\big(\tanh (z_i)\big)\, W_{hh} ∂ h k ​ ∂ h t ​ ​ = i = k + 1 ∏ t ​ diag ( tanh ′ ( z i ​ ) ) W hh ​ This product of ( t − k ) (t-k) ( t − k ) terms is the killer: tanh ⁡ ′ ≤ 1 \tanh \le 1 tanh ′ ≤ 1 always (near 0 when saturated) → multiplying many sub-1 numbers drives the result toward 0 ( vanishing ). W h h W_{hh} W hh ​ raised to the power ( t − k ) (t-k) ( t − k ) scales like its largest singular value λ \lambda λ : λ 1 \lambda 1 λ 1 (with tanh ⁡ ′ ≤ 1 \tanh \le 1 tanh ′ ≤ 1 ) ⇒ \Rightarrow ⇒ vanish; λ 1 \lambda 1 λ 1 is necessary (not sufficient) for the gradient to explode . So early steps contribute almost nothing to the summed gradient — they re heard but they whisper. The loss function (cross-entropy) is fine; the problem is purely getting the signal back through a long multiplicative chain. Truncated BPTT (only unroll the last N N N steps) is the common practical workaround, at the cost of not learning very long dependencies. # 30-second answer An RNN is one cell with shared weights and a single evolving memory; it blends the new input with the carried-over memory and squashes with tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh at each step. Trained with BPTT (backprop on the unrolled, weight-shared chain, summing the shared weights gradients across time). It fails on long sequences because the backward signal is a product of many Jacobians that vanishes (or explodes) — which is the whole motivation for LSTM / GRU gated memory. # See also Cross-Entropy Loss — the output loss (Objectives Losses) Gradient Descent — the optimizer that applies BPTT s gradients (Math) Convolutional Neural Networks — the other core architecture; uses ReLU, RNNs use tanh/sigmoid Next: LSTM GRU — gated fixes for vanishing gradients

text: A cheat-sheet of the concepts covered while working through the TensorGym exercises ( Colab notebook ). # Tensors axes # dim — which axis the operation runs along The number you pass to sum , mean , max , softmax , etc. is the axis that gets collapsed. For a 2D tensor of shape [rows, cols] : dim=0 → travel down the rows → one result per column dim=1 → travel across the columns → one result per row x = torch.tensor([[ 1. , 2 , 3 ], [ 4 , 5 , 6 ]]) # shape [2, 3] torch. sum (x, dim= 0 ) # [5, 7, 9] (per column) torch. sum (x, dim= 1 ) # [6, 15] (per row) Rule of thumb: if the answer should have one number per column, use dim=0 ; per row, dim=1 . # keepdim=True — preserve the collapsed axis as size 1 Keeps shape [2, 1] instead of [2] so it broadcasts back against the original. m = torch. max (x, dim= 1 , keepdim= True ).values # shape [2, 1] x - m # works element-wise per row thanks to broadcasting # squeeze / unsqueeze — remove / add a size-1 dimension v = torch.tensor([ 1 , 2 , 3 ]) # [3] v.unsqueeze( 1 ) # [[1],[2],[3]] shape [3, 1] (column vector) v.unsqueeze( 0 ) # [[1, 2, 3]] shape [1, 3] (row vector) y = torch.tensor([[ 1 ],[ 2 ],[ 3 ]]) # [3, 1] y.squeeze() # [1, 2, 3] shape [3] squeeze only removes dimensions of size 1. keepdim=True is like a built-in unsqueeze . # argmax — index of the max, not the value a = torch.tensor([ 10 , 50 , 30 ]) torch. max (a) # 50 (the value) torch.argmax(a) # 1 (the position). Ties - first occurrence. Same in NumPy. With a dim / axis it returns the argmax along that axis. # torch.cat — join tensors along an axis torch.cat((A[:, :i], A[:, i+ 1 :]), dim= 1 ) # drop column i (join left right blocks) dim=1 joins side-by-side (columns); dim=0 stacks vertically (rows). @ is shorthand for torch.matmul . # dtype gotcha Integer literals make int tensors. mean / var error on int tensors, and mixed-dtype matmul fails. Cast with x = x.float() up front when inputs come from integer lists. # Math foundations # Variance: population ( / N /N / N ) vs unbiased ( / ( N − 1 ) /(N-1) / ( N − 1 ) ) torch.var(x) # default: / (N-1) unbiased (Bessel s correction) torch.var(x, unbiased= False ) # / N population Manual: 1 N ∑ ( x − x ˉ ) 2 \frac{1}{N}\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 N 1 ​ ∑ ( x − x ˉ ) 2 (population) or divide by N − 1 N-1 N − 1 (unbiased). Use population when your data is the whole set (batch norm, standardize); N − 1 N-1 N − 1 when estimating from a sample. # Z-score standardization (per feature/column) x std = x − μ σ 2 + ϵ x_{\text{std}} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} x std ​ = σ 2 + ϵ ​ x − μ ​ mean = x.mean(dim= 0 , keepdim= True ) var = x.var(dim= 0 , unbiased= False , keepdim= True ) x_std = (x - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + 1e-8 ) # 1e-8 for numerical safety # Neural-network building blocks # Softmax (turns logits into a probability distribution) A logit = raw, unbounded model score before normalization. On paper, softmax ( x ) i = e x i ∑ j e x j \text{softmax}(x)_i = \dfrac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}} softmax ( x ) i ​ = ∑ j ​ e x j ​ e x i ​ ​ . m = logits. max (dim= 1 , keepdim= True ).values # subtract max for numerical stability e = torch.exp(logits - m) probs = e / e. sum (dim= 1 , keepdim= True ) # each row sums to 1 The max-subtraction does not change the result (softmax is shift-invariant) — it just prevents exp overflow. # Sigmoid logistic regression σ ( z ) = 1 1 + e − z \sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} σ ( z ) = 1 + e − z 1 ​ squashes any real z z z to ( 0 , 1 ) (0, 1) ( 0 , 1 ) ; a logit of 0 → probability 0.5. logits = X @ w + b probs = torch.sigmoid(logits) # 1 / (1 + e^-z) preds = (probs = 0.5 ). float () # threshold for class labels # Normalization layers (normalize activations, not weights) All re-center/re-scale the values flowing between layers; they differ in what they average over: Method Averages over Batch-size dependent? Batch norm the batch, per feature ( dim=0 ) Yes — noisy for tiny batches Layer norm all features of one example No — used in transformers Group norm feature groups, per example No Batch norm (across the batch / rows): mean = data.mean(dim= 0 ) var = data.var(dim= 0 , unbiased= False ) # BN uses the biased (N) variance out = (data - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + epsilon) The mean/var are statistics computed from data each pass — not learned. Only the weights and the norm s learnable γ \gamma γ (scale) / β \beta β (shift) are updated by gradient descent. Placement is usually: linear → norm → activation (ReLU). # Scaled dot-product attention Attention ( Q , K , V ) = softmax ⁣ ( Q K ⊤ d k ) V \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V Attention ( Q , K , V ) = softmax ( d k ​ ​ Q K ⊤ ​ ) V scores = (query @ key.T) / math.sqrt(query.size(- 1 )) # size(-1) = d_k, the last dim weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=- 1 ) # each query s weights sum to 1 output = weights @ value # weighted blend of value rows Weight the values = weighted average of the value vectors using the softmax weights. title: Cross-Validation
text: Say it in 30s: A way to estimate generalization without wasting data on a fixed validation set. k-fold CV splits the data into k parts, trains on k−1 and validates on the held-out fold, rotates k times, and averages. You get a more stable performance estimate and a sense of its variance. Variants k-fold (k=5 or 10 typical): the default. Stratified k-fold : preserve class ratios per fold — use for imbalanced classification. Leave-one-out : k = n, low bias, high variance, expensive. Group k-fold : keep correlated rows (same user/patient) together to avoid leakage. Time-series split : train on past, validate on future — never shuffle time. Random k-fold leaks the future. Traps Do all preprocessing (scaling, feature selection) inside the fold, or you leak. CV tunes hyperparameters; still keep a final untouched test set. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§8), Time Series Stationarity (§9). Related: Generalization , Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Overfitting Underfitting .
