title: Model Evaluation & Validation
heads: Ranking Metrics: NDCG vs MAP vs MRR
text: The Machine Learning Interview Bible Chapter 5 — Model Evaluation Validation Building a model is half the job; knowing whether it’s any good is the other half, and it’s where most candidates are thinnest. This chapter is about measuring honestly. We start from the confusion matrix that every classification metric is built on, untangle precision from recall and the threshold that trades them, separate ROC-AUC from PR-AUC, cover calibration and ranking metrics, then turn to regression metrics and — crucially — how to split data so your estimate isn’t a lie. The recurring theme: the metric is a modeling decision , and choosing the wrong one is how good models get shipped to do the wrong thing. What you’ll be able to say after this chapter Read a confusion matrix and derive precision, recall, and F1 from it cold. Explain the precision–recall tradeoff and how the threshold moves it. Say exactly when PR-AUC beats ROC-AUC (hint: heavy imbalance). Define calibration and why a well-ranked model can still be dishonest. Choose a cross-validation scheme that respects time and groups — no leakage. # The Confusion Matrix Every classification metric is an arithmetic combination of four counts, so the confusion matrix is the foundation you build everything else on. For a binary problem it cross-tabulates what actually happened against what the model predicted. Four cells, and every classification metric is just a ratio of them. Predicted Positive Predicted Negative Actually Positive True Positive (TP) False Negative (FN) — a miss Actually Negative False Positive (FP) — a false alarm True Negative (TN) The two error types are not interchangeable, and naming them correctly matters. A False Positive (Type I error) is a false alarm — you flagged something that was fine. A False Negative (Type II error) is a miss — you let something real slip through. Which one hurts more is entirely domain-dependent, and that asymmetry is what drives every metric choice in this chapter. Memory hook False Positive = “crying wolf” (Type I). False Negative = “missing the wolf” (Type II). Spam filter: a False Positive eats your real email; a False Negative just lets spam through — so you tune toward avoiding False Positives. Cancer screen: a False Negative is deadly — so you tune toward avoiding those. The cost asymmetry picks the metric. Interview angle Always ask, or state, which error is worse here . Candidates who optimize a model without distinguishing the cost of a miss from the cost of a false alarm signal they’ve never shipped anything. Tie it to the business: “in fraud, a missed fraud costs us the transaction; a false alarm costs a customer’s goodwill — those aren’t equal.” # Classification Metrics From those four cells come the metrics you’ll quote constantly. The danger metric is accuracy — (TP+TN)/total — because it collapses under imbalance: on a dataset that’s 99% negative, “always predict negative” scores 99% and is worthless. Precision and recall are the honest pair. Metric Formula Reads as Use when Accuracy T P + T N all \frac{TP+TN}{\text{all}} all T P + T N ​ Overall correctness Classes are balanced Precision T P T P + F P \frac{TP}{TP+FP} T P + F P T P ​ Of those I flagged, how many were right? False alarms are costly Recall (TPR) T P T P + F N \frac{TP}{TP+FN} T P + F N T P ​ Of the real positives, how many did I catch? Misses are costly F1 2 P R P + R \frac{2PR}{P+R} P + R 2 P R ​ Harmonic mean of P and R Imbalance, want one number Specificity (TNR) T N T N + F P \frac{TN}{TN+FP} T N + F P T N ​ Of the real negatives, how many did I clear? Care about the negative class Precision answers “when I say positive, am I right?” — it’s hurt by false alarms. Recall answers “did I find all the positives?” — it’s hurt by misses. F1 is their harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean, deliberately: the harmonic mean stays low unless both are high, so a model can’t game F1 by maxing one and tanking the other. Memory hook Precision = “of my alarms, how many were real?” Recall = “of the real ones, how many did I sound an alarm for?” Precision polices false alarms; recall polices misses. F1 is the harmonic mean — it refuses to be fooled by one good number. Interview angle Expect “precision or recall for X?” Cancer screening → recall (never miss a case; false alarms get a follow-up test). Spam → precision (never trash a real email). Search results → precision (the top results must be relevant). Say the cost of each error type out loud and the answer falls out. # Threshold: Precision vs Recall Here’s the idea that ties the last section together: most classifiers output a probability , and you turn it into a label by picking a threshold (default 0.5, but that’s just a default). Precision and recall are not fixed properties of the model — they move as you slide the threshold , and they move in opposite directions. Slide the threshold high for precision, low for recall — you can’t max both at once. Raise the threshold and you only flag the cases you’re most sure about: precision climbs, recall falls (you miss the borderline positives). Lower it and you flag aggressively: recall climbs, precision falls (more false alarms). This is the precision–recall tradeoff , and the right threshold is a business decision , not a default — set it by the relative cost of a miss versus a false alarm. Memory hook The threshold is a dial, not a constant. Crank it up → cautious → high precision, low recall. Crank it down → trigger-happy → high recall, low precision. 0.5 is a default, not a law — set it by what an error costs. Interview angle “Your model’s recall is too low — what do you do?” First, cheap: lower the threshold (no retraining needed) and accept the precision hit. Then: resample/reweight for imbalance, add features, or change the model. Reaching for “lower the threshold” first shows you understand that precision and recall are threshold-dependent, not intrinsic. # ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC To judge a model across all thresholds at once, you use an area-under-curve summary. There are two, and knowing when each one lies is a classic senior question. The ROC curve plots True Positive Rate (recall) against False Positive Rate as the threshold sweeps. ROC-AUC is the area under it, interpretable as the probability the model ranks a random positive above a random negative. 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect. The PR curve plots Precision against Recall over the same sweep, and PR-AUC is its area. ROC can look great on imbalanced data; PR tells the truth because precision feels the flood of negatives. ROC-AUC PR-AUC Axes TPR vs FPR Precision vs Recall Baseline (random) 0.5 always The positive class prevalence Sensitive to imbalance? No — can look misleadingly good Yes — reflects rare-class difficulty Use when Classes roughly balanced; care about both classes Positive class is rare and is what you care about The key insight: FPR has the huge negative count in its denominator , so on imbalanced data a flood of false positives barely moves it — ROC-AUC stays optimistically high. Precision has the false positives in its denominator without the true negatives , so it feels every false alarm. When positives are rare and they’re what you care about (fraud, disease, click prediction), PR-AUC is the honest summary . Memory hook On a needle-in-a-haystack problem, ROC-AUC flatters and PR-AUC tells the truth. ROC dilutes false positives in a sea of true negatives; precision doesn’t get to hide them. Rare positive class → trust PR-AUC. Interview angle “You have 1% fraud and ROC-AUC is 0.95 — are you happy?” The trap is yes. Strong answer: ROC-AUC is inflated by the 99% negatives; check PR-AUC and the precision/recall at your operating threshold before celebrating. This single distinction is one of the most reliable senior-vs-junior separators in evaluation. # Calibration Ranking well and being honest about probabilities are different things, and the gap is calibration. A model is calibrated if, among all the times it says “0.7,” the event really happens about 70% of the time. AUC only cares about order ; calibration cares about whether the number means what it says . A calibrated model’s confidence matches reality; the diagonal is perfect. This matters whenever you act on the probability itself — expected-value decisions, pricing, risk thresholds, or feeding the score into downstream math. A model can have great AUC and terrible calibration: it ranks cases correctly but is systematically over- or under-confident. You diagnose it with a reliability diagram (predicted probability vs observed frequency) and fix it on held-out data with Platt scaling (fit a sigmoid) or isotonic regression (a flexible monotonic fit). Model Calibration out of the box Note Logistic regression Usually good Trained on log-loss; can drift if heavily regularized, reweighted or misspecified Naive Bayes Poor Independence assumption pushes probs to 0/1 SVM Uncalibrated scores (no probabilities) Needs Platt scaling Deep nets / boosted trees Deep nets: often overconfident; boosted trees/RF: often distorted (sigmoid-shaped, underconfident) Check a reliability diagram; calibrate if you act on the number Memory hook Calibration is honesty, not accuracy. “When I say 70%, does it happen 70% of the time?” AUC grades the ranking ; calibration grades the number . A model can ace one and flunk the other. Go deeper (optional) Don’t conflate calibration with discrimination (AUC). You can have perfect ranking and awful calibration (just squash all scores toward 0.5) or perfect calibration and poor ranking. If you only need to threshold or rank , calibration may not matter; if you multiply the probability into a decision , it’s essential. # Ranking Metrics: NDCG vs MAP vs MRR When the output is an ordered list — search, recommendations, retrieval — accuracy and AUC miss the point: what matters is whether the good items are near the top . Three metrics dominate, differing in what they reward. Metric Rewards Use when MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) The rank of the first relevant item One right answer (Q A, “I’m feeling lucky”) MAP (Mean Average Precision) Precision across all relevant items, binary relevance Multiple relevant items, relevant-or-not NDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) Graded relevance, discounted by position Items have degrees of relevance (star ratings) All three share the position-discount instinct: a relevant result at rank 1 is worth more than the same result at rank 10. NDCG is the most general because it handles graded relevance (a 5-star match beats a 3-star match) and normalizes against the ideal ordering, so scores are comparable across queries. MRR is the simplest — just 1/(rank of the first hit) — and fits “single correct answer” tasks. Memory hook MRR cares only about the first good hit. MAP cares about all the good hits, present-or-absent. NDCG cares about all of them and how good each is , discounted by position. Increasing sophistication: first → all → all-and-graded. Interview angle “How would you evaluate a recommender?” Don’t say accuracy. Say a ranking metric and justify it: NDCG if you have graded feedback (ratings, watch time), MAP for binary relevance with several right answers, MRR if there’s essentially one. Then mention that offline ranking metrics are a proxy — the real test is an online A/B on engagement (Chapter 14). # Regression Metrics For continuous targets the question shifts to how far off, on average , and the choice among metrics is mostly about how you want to treat large errors and whether you want a unit-free score. Metric Behavior Use when MAE Mean absolute error; robust to outliers Outliers shouldn’t dominate; want error in original units MSE Mean squared error; punishes large errors hard Big misses are especially bad RMSE √MSE; same units as the target, still outlier-sensitive Want MSE’s penalty but readable units R² Fraction of variance explained (1 = perfect, 0 = mean-baseline) Want a unit-free “how much better than guessing the mean” The core tradeoff is MAE vs MSE/RMSE : squaring makes MSE punish big errors disproportionately, so it’s the right choice when a single large miss is unacceptable — but that same squaring makes it sensitive to outliers , which MAE shrugs off. R² rescales error against a “predict the mean” baseline, giving a unit-free score, but it can be misleadingly high on a strong trend and even go negative when the model is worse than the mean. (Adjusted R², which penalizes adding useless features, is covered in Chapter 3.) Memory hook MAE treats all errors fairly (robust). MSE/RMSE square the error, so it obsesses over the big misses (outlier-sensitive). R² answers “how much better than just guessing the average?” — unit-free, but can flatter you. Interview angle “MAE or RMSE?” Answer with the outlier story: RMSE if large errors are disproportionately costly and the data is clean; MAE if outliers exist and you don’t want a few of them to dictate the model. If asked why a model has R² of 0.0 — it’s no better than predicting the mean; negative R² means worse than the mean. # Cross-Validation: How to Split Data A single train/test split gives a noisy estimate — you got lucky or unlucky with which points landed in test. Cross-validation averages over several splits for a stabler estimate, but the way you split must respect the structure of your data, or you leak the future into the past and your metric becomes a fantasy. k-fold rotates the test fold; but time and groups demand special splits. Scheme How it works Use when k-fold Split into k folds; each takes a turn as test Standard i.i.d. tabular data Stratified k-fold k-fold preserving class proportions in each fold Classification, especially imbalanced Leave-One-Out k = n; each point is its own test fold Tiny datasets (expensive) Time-series split Always train on past, test on future Temporal data — never shuffle Group k-fold Keep each entity entirely in one fold Repeated users/patients/docs The two splits that prevent leakage are the ones interviewers probe. Time-series CV never shuffles — you train on the past and test on the future, because random shuffling would let the model “see tomorrow” to predict today. Group CV keeps all rows of one entity (a patient, a user) together, so the model can’t memorize an individual in training and get credit for “predicting” them in test. And the golden rule from Chapter 0 still binds: fit every preprocessing step (scaling, imputation) inside the training fold only , then apply it to the validation fold. Memory hook k-fold for ordinary data. Stratify when classes are imbalanced. Split by time for time series (never peek at the future). Split by group when the same entity repeats (never let it sit on both sides). The wrong split = silent leakage = a beautiful, lying score. Interview angle “How would you cross-validate a model that predicts next month’s sales?” The trap is plain k-fold. Right answer: a time-based split — train on earlier periods, validate on later ones, never shuffle — because shuffling leaks future information and inflates the score. Mention that preprocessing stats must be fit on the training fold only. Rapid Fire — Evaluation amp; Validation Confusion matrix: TP/FP/FN/TN. False Positive = Type I (false alarm); False Negative = Type II (miss). Cost asymmetry picks the metric. - Accuracy lies under imbalance. Precision = of my alarms how many were real; Recall = of the real ones how many I caught; F1 = harmonic mean. - Threshold slides precision vs recall in opposite directions; 0.5 is a default, set it by error costs. - ROC-AUC flatters on imbalanced data (FPR hides false positives in true negatives); PR-AUC is honest when positives are rare. - Calibration = “when I say 70% it happens 70%.” AUC grades ranking, calibration grades the number; fix with Platt/isotonic. - Ranking: MRR (first hit) → MAP (all hits, binary) → NDCG (graded + position-discounted). - Regression: MAE robust; MSE/RMSE punish big errors and feel outliers; R² = variance explained vs the mean. - Cross-validation: stratify for imbalance, split by time for temporal data, split by group for repeated entities; fit preprocessing on the train fold only. # Which Metric When The chapter in one table — match the metric to the problem, because the metric is the objective you’re really optimizing. Problem Metric Balanced classification Accuracy (or AUC) Imbalanced classification PR-AUC, F1, precision/recall at threshold Cost of a miss ≫ false alarm Optimize recall Cost of a false alarm ≫ miss Optimize precision Acting on the probability value Calibration (reliability diagram + Platt/isotonic) Ranking / search / recommendation NDCG, MAP, or MRR Regression, clean data, punish big errors RMSE Regression with outliers MAE “How much better than the mean?” R² The closing principle ties the chapter to Chapter 0: separate the offline ML metric (what you compute on held-out data) from the online business metric (what you A/B test in production). A model that wins on offline AUC can still lose on revenue or engagement — so the metric you optimize must be a faithful proxy for the value you actually care about. Interview angle The unifying senior insight: choosing the metric is a modeling decision, made before you train. For any “how would you evaluate X?” answer in two layers — the offline metric tied to the error costs, and the online metric (A/B test on the business outcome) that’s the real arbiter. Saying “I’d pick the metric from what an error costs the business” is the line that lands. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember Confusion matrix TP/FP/FN/TN; FP = Type I (false alarm), FN = Type II (miss). Accuracy trap Useless under imbalance — “always negative” scores high and is worthless. Precision vs recall Precision = of my alarms how many real; recall = of the real ones how many caught. F1 Harmonic mean of precision and recall — both must be high. Threshold A dial that trades precision against recall; 0.5 is a default, set it by error cost. ROC vs PR AUC ROC-AUC flatters on imbalance; PR-AUC is honest when positives are rare. Calibration “When I say 70% it happens 70%” — AUC grades ranking, calibration grades the number. Ranking metrics MRR (first hit) → MAP (all hits) → NDCG (graded, position-discounted). Regression metrics MAE robust; RMSE punishes big errors / feels outliers; R² = variance explained. Cross-validation Stratify for imbalance, split by time for temporal, by group for repeats; fit preprocessing on train fold only. Which metric Match it to error costs; separate the offline metric from the online business metric. # Related Precision Recall ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC Cross-Validation Bias-Variance Tradeoff

title: Precision & Recall
text: Say it in 30s: Precision = of the things I flagged positive, how many were right (TP / (TP+FP)) — punishes false alarms. Recall = of the actual positives, how many did I catch (TP / (TP+FN)) — punishes misses. They trade off as you move the decision threshold. When to favor which Recall when missing a positive is costly: cancer screening, fraud, safety. Precision when a false alarm is costly: spam filters, recommending an expensive action. F1 = harmonic mean of the two, for a single number when you care about both. The threshold link Lower threshold → more positives → higher recall, lower precision. Raise it → the reverse. This is why you report the PR curve , not a single point, on imbalanced problems. Traps Accuracy is misleading under class imbalance (99% negatives → predict all-negative scores 99%). Precision/recall ignore true negatives by design — that s the point. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§2–3). Related: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC , Logistic Regression , Bias-Variance Tradeoff .

title: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC
text: Say it in 30s: Both summarize a classifier across all thresholds. ROC plots TPR vs FPR; its AUC is the probability a random positive is ranked above a random negative. PR plots precision vs recall. On imbalanced data, prefer PR-AUC — ROC-AUC looks deceptively good because the huge negative class makes FPR tiny. Key points ROC-AUC = 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect; threshold-independent and class-balance-insensitive (which is both a feature and a bug). PR-AUC baseline is the positive class prevalence, so it honestly reflects rarity. Use ROC-AUC to compare rankers in general; switch to PR-AUC when positives are rare and false positives matter (fraud, retrieval, medical). Trap: quoting a 0.95 ROC-AUC on a 1%-positive problem can hide poor precision at the operating point — show PR-AUC too. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§4). Related: Precision Recall , Logistic Regression .

title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
text: Say it in 30s: For squared-error regression, expected test error decomposes exactly into bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Bias is error from wrong assumptions (too simple a model, underfits); variance is error from sensitivity to the training sample (too flexible a model, overfits). Lowering one usually raises the other, so the goal is the sweet spot, not zero of either. Key points More capacity (deeper tree, higher polynomial degree, less regularization) → lower bias, higher variance. More data lets you afford more capacity without paying as much variance. The dartboard picture: bias = is the cluster centered on the target; variance = how tight the cluster is. The U-curve: total test error falls then rises as complexity grows; minimum = optimal capacity. Modern asterisk: double descent — past the interpolation point, very overparameterized models can improve again. Common follow-ups / traps How do you reduce variance? → more data, regularization, simpler model, bagging/ensembling. How do you reduce bias? → richer model, better features, boosting. Don t confuse this with the bias/variance of an estimator in statistics (related, not identical framing). See depth: Fundamentals (§4). Related: Overfitting Underfitting , Regularization , Cross-Validation , Bagging vs Boosting .

title: Empirical Risk Minimization
text: Say it in 30s: We want to minimize true risk — expected loss over the real data distribution — but we can t see that distribution. So we minimize empirical risk , the average loss on our training sample, as a stand-in. ERM is pick the hypothesis with lowest average training loss. Why it works (and when it doesn t) Justified by the i.i.d. assumption : training and future data come from the same distribution, so empirical risk estimates true risk. Pure ERM overfits, so in practice we use regularized risk minimization : empirical loss + λ·penalty. When i.i.d. breaks (distribution shift, autocorrelated time series, sampling bias), empirical risk becomes an optimistic, misleading estimate. Trap: minimizing training loss is the means , not the goal. The goal is low true risk = generalization. See depth: Fundamentals (§2). Related: Generalization , Regularization , Maximum Likelihood Estimation .

title: Fundamentals
heads: Generalization: Why Held-Out Data Is Sacred
Regularization, Inductive Bias  No Free Lunch
Turning a vague problem into a crisp one: I-O-L-M
text: Foundations: the learning problem. Simplified illustrated edition. This is the bedrock the rest stands on. We answer four questions: what machine learning actually is , how supervised learning is set up as an optimization problem, why held-out data is sacred, and what the bias-variance tradeoff really means. Nail these and most fundamentals round questions become a handful of ideas you apply, not facts you memorize. What you #39;ll be able to say after this chapter Define ML as function approximation under a generalization constraint . Name the five learning settings by their supervision signal . Explain why we minimize empirical risk but care about true risk. Diagnose underfitting vs overfitting from a learning curve. Turn any vague use ML for X prompt into a crisp problem with I-O-L-M . # What Machine Learning Is Classical software is rules in, answers out : a human writes the logic, the computer applies it. Machine learning flips the second half: answers in, rules out . You hand it worked examples and it reverse-engineers an approximate procedure. Classical code applies rules you wrote; ML infers the rules from examples. Why bother? For a huge class of problems nobody can write the rules by hand: telling a cat from a dog in pixels, predicting loan default, translating English to Japanese. The rules exist in human intuition but are too tangled to articulate. ML recovers an approximation of them from data. One subtlety to carry through: ML never learns the true rule. It learns a function that fits the data you showed it and, hopefully, behaves well on data you haven t. That gap between fits what I saw and works on what I haven t seen is the single most important theme in the field. Regularization, validation, and the bias-variance tradeoff are all machinery for managing it. Memory hook Classical programming = rules in, answers out . Machine learning = answers in, rules out . Interview angle What is machine learning? is a softball you can fumble. Weak: computers learning from data. Strong: we use data to pick a function from a hypothesis space, and we care about expected performance on unseen data, not training accuracy. Saying generalization in your first sentence signals seniority. # The five learning settings Learning problems are grouped by what kind of supervision signal the algorithm gets — how much, and what kind of, labeled feedback is available. The map of learning settings, organized by supervision signal. Setting Supervision signal Goal Examples Supervised Labeled ( x , y ) (x, y) ( x , y ) pairs Learn a mapping x → y x \to y x → y that generalizes Spam detection, credit scoring, demand forecasting Unsupervised Inputs only, no labels Find structure in the data Clustering, PCA/UMAP, density estimation Self-supervised Labels forged from the input itself Pretrain rich representations BERT (mask a word), GPT (next token), contrastive image learning Semi-supervised Few labels + lots of unlabeled data Spread few labels over data structure Pseudo-labeling, label propagation Reinforcement Reward from an environment Learn a policy maximizing cumulative reward AlphaGo, robotics, RLHF Memory hook Self-supervised learning is supervised learning that forges its own labels : hide a piece of the input, predict it, repeat a billion times. It s the engine behind foundation models. Interview angle A classic trap: is this supervised or unsupervised? for an ambiguous task. Don t name a box — name the supervision signal . Recommendation can be supervised (predict the rating), self-supervised (predict the next item), or RL (optimize long-term engagement). The signal is the discriminator. Go deeper (optional) The boundaries are porous. The dominant modern recipe — self-supervised pretraining then supervised fine-tuning — is neither purely one nor the other. Treat the taxonomy as vocabulary for describing the components of a system, not exclusive boxes. # Discriminative vs generative models A second axis, orthogonal to supervision, cuts across how a model represents the problem. People fumble this one constantly. Discriminative models draw the border; generative models learn each class s shape and derive the border. Discriminative Generative Learns p ( y ∣ x ) p(y \mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) — or just a decision boundary p ( x , y ) = p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) p(x, y) = p(x \mid y)\,p(y) p ( x , y ) = p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) — the full data story Answers Which side of the line is this? How is each class generated? then applies Bayes rule Can it sample? No Yes — can generate new x x x , detect outliers, handle missing features Examples Logistic regression, SVM, random forest, most NN classifiers Naive Bayes, GMM, HMM, VAE, diffusion, autoregressive LLMs Wins when You only need the label and have ample data Small data (assumptions hold), or you need to sample Memory hook Discriminative draws the border ; generative paints the countries . Generative knows enough to forge a new passport (sample data); discriminative only checks which side of the line you re on. Go deeper (optional) Ng Jordan s classic result: a generative model (Naive Bayes) has higher asymptotic error than its discriminative pair (logistic regression), but reaches that asymptote with far fewer samples. So generative can win in the small-data regime and lose in the large-data regime — they converge to different places at different speeds. Rapid fire — What ML is ML infers rules from examples; classical code applies hand-written rules. Reframe what is ML as function approximation under a generalization constraint . Five settings by supervision signal: supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement. Self-supervised = supervised with manufactured labels; it powers foundation models. Discriminative models p ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) (border); generative models p ( x , y ) p(x,y) p ( x , y ) (countries, can sample). Generative wins small-data / sampling; discriminative wins large-data accuracy. # The Supervised Setup, Formally The formalism is exactly what separates a crisp answer from hand-waving. Supervised learning has six objects: Object What it is Example Input space X \mathcal{X} X The set of possible inputs Feature vectors, images, sentences Output space Y \mathcal{Y} Y The set of possible labels { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} { 0 , 1 } for binary, R \mathbb{R} R for regression Distribution D \mathcal{D} D Unknown source of all data; we only see samples The real world we never observe directly Training set S S S n n n examples drawn i.i.d. from D \mathcal{D} D Your labeled dataset Hypothesis space H \mathcal{H} H Functions h : X → Y h : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y} h : X → Y you re willing to consider Linear models? Depth-3 trees? A given NN? Loss ℓ ( h ( x ) , y ) \ell(h(x), y) ℓ ( h ( x ) , y ) How wrong a single prediction is Squared loss, 0-1 loss, cross-entropy The goal: use S S S to pick an h h h that performs well on the whole distribution D \mathcal{D} D , not just on S S S . # True risk vs empirical risk What we actually care about is the true risk — the average loss over the entire distribution, R ( h ) = E [ ℓ ( h ( x ) , y ) ] R(h) = \mathbb{E}[\ell(h(x), y)] R ( h ) = E [ ℓ ( h ( x ) , y )] for a fresh example drawn from the real world. The problem is fatal: we cannot compute it , because we don t have D \mathcal{D} D , only the finite sample S S S . So we approximate it with the only data we have — the average loss on the training set. This is the empirical risk : R S ( h ) = 1 n ∑ i = 1 n ℓ ( h ( x i ) , y i ) R_S(h) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell(h(x_i), y_i) R S ​ ( h ) = n 1 ​ i = 1 ∑ n ​ ℓ ( h ( x i ​ ) , y i ​ ) By the law of large numbers, for a fixed h h h it converges to the true risk as n n n grows. It s the visible shadow cast by the invisible true risk. True risk R ( h ) R(h) R ( h ) Empirical risk R S ( h ) R_S(h) R S ​ ( h ) Defined over The whole distribution D \mathcal{D} D The finite training sample S S S Can we compute it? No — D \mathcal{D} D is unknown Yes — it s just an average Role What we want to minimize The proxy we actually minimize Catch Invisible Unbiased but noisy for a fixed h h h ; optimistically biased for the h h h picked by minimizing it # Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) Since we can t minimize the true risk directly, we minimize the empirical risk instead. That principle is Empirical Risk Minimization : pick the hypothesis with the smallest average error on your training data. Almost every model you ve trained does a version of this — linear regression minimizes squared loss, logistic regression minimizes log-loss, a neural net minimizes cross-entropy via SGD. ERM minimizes the wiggly empirical risk, but the minimum we actually want belongs to the smooth true risk. Here s the crucial gap: ERM minimizes R S R_S R S ​ , but we want to minimize R R R , and the minimizer of one isn t the minimizer of the other. When H \mathcal{H} H is rich and n n n is small, R S R_S R S ​ can hit zero (perfect training fit) while R R R stays large. That is overfitting , and it s why naive ERM on an unconstrained H \mathcal{H} H fails. Managing this gap is the entire game. Memory hook True risk is your score on the real exam; empirical risk is your score on the practice test. ERM means study to ace the practice test — it works only if the practice test resembles the real one and you didn t memorize the answer key. Interview angle What does training a model actually do? Senior answer: it performs regularized empirical risk minimization over a chosen hypothesis space, using the training sample as a proxy for the unknown distribution — and the whole challenge is that the proxy is imperfect, which is why we hold out data and regularize. Rapid fire — Supervised setup Objects: input space X \mathcal{X} X , output space Y \mathcal{Y} Y , distribution D \mathcal{D} D , i.i.d. sample S S S , hypothesis space H \mathcal{H} H , loss ℓ \ell ℓ . True risk R ( h ) = E [ ℓ ] R(h) = \mathbb{E}[\ell] R ( h ) = E [ ℓ ] is what we want but can t compute. Empirical risk R S ( h ) = 1 n ∑ ℓ R_S(h) = \frac{1}{n}\sum\ell R S ​ ( h ) = n 1 ​ ∑ ℓ is the computable proxy. ERM picks the hypothesis minimizing empirical risk; nearly all training is regularized ERM. The gap between R R R and R S R_S R S ​ is the source of overfitting and the reason for held-out data. # Generalization: Why Held-Out Data Is Sacred Generalization is performance on data the model wasn t trained on. It s the only thing that matters: a model that memorizes its training set and fails on everything else is worthless. This section is about measuring it honestly — mostly a matter of discipline. # The i.i.d. assumption The license to even hope for generalization is the assumption that training and future data are drawn i.i.d. from the same distribution D \mathcal{D} D . Identically distributed : test data looks statistically like training data. Independent : examples don t leak information about each other. When this breaks — the world shifts after you train, the test set comes from a different population, a time series is autocorrelated — generalization estimates turn optimistic and models silently degrade. Distribution shift is the number-one reason good offline models disappoint in production. Memory hook i.i.d. is the contract that says the future will be sampled from the same urn as the past. Every ML guarantee is voided the moment that contract breaks. # The train / validation / test split Because training error is an optimistically biased estimate of true risk, we estimate generalization on data the model never saw while fitting. Standard practice splits three ways. Three-way split (left) and the learning curve whose gap diagnoses bias vs variance (right). Split Typical % What it s for Training ~60–80% Fit the parameters (weights). The model directly minimizes loss here. Validation ~10–20% Tune hyperparameters and make model decisions: architecture, regularization, when to stop, which features. Test ~10–20% Used once , at the very end, for an honest unbiased estimate of real-world performance. Why do we need both validation and test? Every time you use the validation score to make a decision, you fit it a little. After trying a hundred configurations and keeping the best, the winner s validation score is optimistic — you ve partly overfit the validation set through selection. The untouched test set restores honesty. The golden rule Never touch the test set until the very end. Not to peek, not to just check, not to engineer features, not to pick a threshold. The moment a test observation influences any decision, the test set stops being an unbiased estimate and becomes just another training signal. Treat it as locked in a vault. Violating this is called data snooping (or leakage). It s insidious: it inflates your reported metrics while the model is secretly worse. The classic traps: Leakage type What goes wrong Fix Preprocessing on full data Normalization stats / imputation / feature ranks computed before the split leak test info into training Fit every transform on the training fold only , then apply Target leakage A feature is a proxy for or downstream of the label (e.g. account closed date for churn) Drop features unknown at prediction time Temporal leakage Random shuffling trains on the future to predict the past Always split by time for temporal problems Group leakage Same patient/user/doc in both train and test; model memorizes the entity Split by group Interview angle Your model scores 99% offline but tanks in production. What happened? Walk the checklist: distribution shift, target leakage, temporal/group leakage, normalization fit on full data, validation overfitting from too many trials. A systematic suspicion of suspiciously good numbers is the senior instinct interviewers screen for. # Reading a learning curve A learning curve plots error against training-set size (or epochs). It s a cheap diagnostic. As you add data, training error rises slightly and validation error falls; the two converge, and the vertical gap between them is the generalization gap . What you see What it means → the fix Big gap that doesn t close with more data High variance / overfitting → more data, more regularization, or a simpler model Both curves plateau high and sit close together High bias / underfitting → a more expressive model or better features (more data won t help) Rapid fire — Generalization Generalization = performance on unseen data; it s the only goal. i.i.d. (same distribution, independent samples) licenses generalization; distribution shift breaks it. Train fits parameters, validation tunes choices, test is the one-shot honest estimate. You need both val and test because repeated validation selection overfits the validation set. Golden rule: never touch the test set until the end. Leakage (preprocessing on full data, target/temporal/group) inflates offline metrics and kills production. Learning curve: persistent gap = variance; high converged floor = bias. # Overfitting, Underfitting the Bias-Variance Tradeoff Underfitting : the model is too simple to capture the pattern — high error on both train and test. Overfitting : the model is so flexible it captures noise as if it were signal — low train error, high test error. The art of ML is steering between the two. The same 18 noisy points fit by polynomials of degree 1, 4, and 14. Note the overfit model has the lowest training error and the worst test error. Model capacity (complexity) is the knob: polynomial degree, tree depth, number of NN parameters, the inverse of regularization strength. Low capacity → underfit; high capacity → overfit; the right spot depends on how much data you have (more data supports more capacity). Memory hook Underfitting is a student who didn t study (wrong on practice and exam). Overfitting is a student who memorized the practice answer key (perfect on practice, lost on the exam). You want the one who learned the concept . # The bias-variance decomposition For squared-error regression the tradeoff is exact. If data is y = f ( x ) + ε y = f(x) + \varepsilon y = f ( x ) + ε with zero-mean noise of variance σ 2 \sigma^2 σ 2 , then the expected error at a point, averaged over all training sets you might draw, splits cleanly: E [ ( y − f ^ ( x ) ) 2 ] = Bias 2 ⏟ too simple + Variance ⏟ too flexible + σ 2 ⏟ irreducible \mathbb{E}\big[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2\big] = \underbrace{\text{Bias}^2}_{\text{too simple}} + \underbrace{\text{Variance}}_{\text{too flexible}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}} E [ ( y − f ^ ​ ( x ) ) 2 ] = too simple Bias 2 ​ ​ + too flexible Variance ​ ​ + irreducible σ 2 ​ ​ Term Plain English Signals Bias² How far the average prediction sits from the truth — systematic error in the same direction Model too simple Variance How much the prediction jumps around as you swap training sets Model too flexible, chasing noise σ 2 \sigma^2 σ 2 (noise) The floor — the label is partly random; no model beats it Irreducible The tension: simplifying lowers variance but raises bias ; enriching lowers bias but raises variance . You can t drive both to zero with finite data — push one down and the other comes up. Total error is their sum, so you minimize by trading off. Go deeper (optional) The clean additive split is special to squared loss . For 0-1 loss or cross-entropy the decomposition is messier and not additive the same way — a subtlety interviewers occasionally test. Don t claim bias-variance decomposes cleanly for classification accuracy: it doesn t. # The dartboard picture The most durable mental image: throwing darts at a target. The bullseye is the truth; each dart is a prediction from a model trained on one random dataset. Bias is aim (is the cluster centered?); variance is grouping (how tight is it?). Memory hook Bias = aim (is the cluster centered on the bullseye?). Variance = grouping (how tight is the cluster?). A sniper with a bent scope: low variance, high bias. A jittery shooter with good aim: low bias, high variance. # The U-curve Plot expected test error against complexity and you get the famous U. As complexity rises, bias² falls steeply but variance climbs; their sum plus the noise floor is U-shaped. The minimum is the optimal capacity for your data. Bias falls and variance rises with complexity; total error bottoms out at the sweet spot. Training error (not shown) keeps falling monotonically to the right — which is exactly why you can t pick complexity by training error . You pick it by validation error, which traces this U. Interview angle — which lever moves which term Expect how do you reduce variance without adding much bias? Knowing which lever moves which term is the actual test. To reduce VARIANCE (overfitting) To reduce BIAS (underfitting) More data A richer / more expressive model Bagging / ensembling (averages variance away) Boosting (fits the residual error) Regularization (trades a little bias for a lot of variance) Better features / less regularization # Double descent — the modern asterisk The clean U is the classical story, and mostly right. But in modern deep learning, as you grow a model past the point where it can perfectly fit (interpolate) the training data, test error often goes down again after a spike at the interpolation threshold . Double descent: error dips, spikes where the model exactly fits the data, then dips a second time. This is why a neural net with far more parameters than data points can still generalize beautifully. The leading explanation: among the many settings that perfectly fit the data, gradient descent has an implicit bias toward simple, low-norm solutions — so huge models effectively self-regularize. Go deeper (optional) Don t oversell this as overfitting isn t real. The classical U holds for a fixed effective complexity; double descent is a phenomenon of overparameterized interpolating models with optimizer-induced regularization. Both pictures are true in their regimes — saying so reads as well-calibrated rather than buzzword-chasing. Rapid fire — Bias, variance, capacity Underfit = high train AND test error (high bias). Overfit = low train, high test (high variance). Capacity (degree, depth, #params, 1/regularization) is the knob; more data supports more capacity. Squared error = = = Bias² + Variance + σ 2 \sigma^2 σ 2 (this clean split is special to squared loss). Bias = aim off-center; variance = loose grouping; noise = the floor you can t beat. U-curve: pick the minimum via validation error, never training error. Lower variance: more data, bagging, regularization. Lower bias: richer model, boosting, better features. Double descent: overparameterized nets can improve again past the interpolation threshold. # Regularization, Inductive Bias No Free Lunch Three tightly linked ideas explain why and how we deliberately constrain models. Idea What it means Regularization Any change to learning that reduces variance/overfitting, usually by penalizing complexity. Minimize R S ( h ) + λ Ω ( h ) R_S(h) + \lambda\,\Omega(h) R S ​ ( h ) + λ Ω ( h ) instead of R S ( h ) R_S(h) R S ​ ( h ) alone, where Ω \Omega Ω measures complexity ( ∥ w ∥ 2 \lVert w\rVert^2 ∥ w ∥ 2 ridge, ∥ w ∥ 1 \lVert w\rVert_1 ∥ w ∥ 1 ​ lasso) and λ \lambda λ sets the strength. It trades a little bias for a larger drop in variance — sliding you left toward the U-curve s sweet spot. Early stopping, dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, and ensembling are all regularizers in spirit. Inductive bias The assumptions a model uses to generalize beyond the data. Every model that generalizes has one. A linear model assumes linearity; a CNN assumes locality and translation invariance; an RNN/Transformer assumes sequence structure; a tree assumes axis-aligned splits. It s not a flaw — it s what lets a model prefer one of the infinitely many functions consistent with finite data. No Free Lunch Averaged over all possible problems, no learner beats any other. Any algorithm that excels on one class of problems must do correspondingly worse on another. There is no universally best model — so your job is to match the model s inductive bias to your problem s structure . Memory hook Inductive bias is the model s prejudice about what good functions look like before it sees data. Convolution s prejudice: a feature means the same thing wherever it appears. Pick a model whose prejudices fit your problem. Interview angle What s the best ML algorithm? The trap is naming one. Invoke No Free Lunch: there s no best algorithm in general; the right choice depends on the data s structure, size, and the inductive bias that fits — which is why we validate empirically rather than reason to a single winner. Deep nets crush vision/language because their biases (hierarchy, locality, compositionality) fit that data; on heterogeneous tabular data, gradient-boosted trees often win. Rapid fire — Regularization amp; NFL Regularization = penalize complexity ( R S + λ Ω R_S + \lambda\Omega R S ​ + λ Ω ) to trade a little bias for a lot of variance reduction. Early stopping, dropout, weight decay, augmentation, ensembling are all variance-fighting regularizers. Inductive bias = built-in assumptions about plausible functions; it s what makes generalization possible. No Free Lunch: averaged over all problems, all learners tie — so match the model to the problem. There is no universally best algorithm; this is why we validate empirically. # Method Taxonomies to Speak Fluently A few orthogonal axes for classifying methods come up constantly. Speaking them fluently signals breadth. Axis Option A Option B Parametric vs nonparametric Parametric: fixed #params regardless of data size; can discard the data (linear/logistic regression, a fixed NN). Strong assumptions, fast, data-efficient, can underfit. Nonparametric: effective #params grows with data (kNN, kernels, trees, GPs). Flexible, fewer assumptions, data/compute hungry, can overfit. ( ≠ \ne  = zero parameters.) Batch vs online Batch/offline: train on all data at once, deploy a fixed model. Mini-batch SGD is still batch — an optimization detail, not online. Online: update incrementally per example/mini-batch. Suits streaming and non-stationary data; adapts to drift but can be unstable. Problem framing Classification (discrete label; accuracy, AUC), Regression (continuous; MSE, MAE, R 2 R^2 R 2 ) Ranking (relative order; NDCG, MAP, MRR), Generation (structured output; perplexity, human eval) Memory hook Parametric pours the data into a fixed-size mold and discards it. Nonparametric keeps the data and grows with it — kNN is the extreme: the model is literally the training set. The same business problem can often be framed multiple ways, and choosing the framing is itself a modeling decision . Recommend items can be classification (click / no-click), regression (predict rating), or ranking — and the ranking framing usually matches the real objective best. Axis Option A Option B Pick A when… Params Parametric (linreg, fixed NN) Nonparametric (kNN, trees, GP) Limited data, a structural prior, need speed/small footprint Training Batch / offline Online / incremental Data is static, fits in memory, no drift (B for streaming) Output Classification / Regression Ranking / Generation Answer is one discrete/continuous target (ranking when order is the goal) Model Discriminative Generative You only need the label and have ample data (generative to sample / small data) Rapid fire — Method taxonomies Parametric = fixed #params, can discard data; nonparametric = #params grow with data. Nonparametric ≠ \ne  = zero params. Parametric: efficient, strong assumptions, may underfit. Nonparametric: flexible, hungry, may overfit. Batch trains on all data at once; online updates per example. Mini-batch SGD is still batch. Output type sets the loss + metric: classification, regression, ranking, generation. Framing the business problem (classification vs regression vs ranking) is itself a key modeling decision. # The End-to-End ML Workflow Interviews increasingly test whether you can operate , not just recite algorithms. The lifecycle is the same everywhere, and narrating it crisply is its own skill. The ML lifecycle. The amateur sprints to Iterate ; the pro invests in Frame and Data. Stage What happens (and where people slip) 1. Frame Turn a vague business goal into a precise ML problem. Highest-leverage and most-skipped step. 2. Data Collect, clean, label, understand; build features; set up the split (respecting time/groups). Most time goes here; most failures originate here. 3. Baseline Build the dumbest reasonable model first (majority class, a linear model, a heuristic). It calibrates expectations and exposes leakage. Skipping it is a classic junior mistake. 4. Iterate Improve via features, models, tuning — one change at a time. Use the validation set. Diagnose with learning curves to know which lever to pull. 5. Evaluate Measure against the business-aligned metric on held-out data, with error analysis by slice. Touch the test set once , here. 6. Deploy monitor Ship it, then watch for distribution shift, drift, latency, degradation. Production is where i.i.d. assumptions go to die. Plan retraining. Memory hook Frame → Data → Baseline → Iterate → Evaluate → Deploy. Amateurs sprint to the fun modeling; pros invest in Frame and Data, build a Baseline before anything fancy, and treat Deploy/monitor as half the job. # Turning a vague problem into a crisp one: I-O-L-M This separates levels in interviews. We want to reduce customer churn — how would you use ML? The wrong move is naming algorithms. The right move is defining the ML problem by pinning down four things. Question to answer Churn example I — Input What features exist at prediction time ? (A feature known only after the event is leakage.) Usage frequency, tenure, support tickets, plan type, recent activity trend O — Output What exactly are you predicting, in what form, over what horizon? Probability an active subscriber cancels within the next 30 days → calibrated classification L — Label source Where does ground truth come from? Is it reliable, available, unbiased? Did this customer cancel in the 30-day window? — from historical billing logs M — Metric How is success measured, tied to business value? Precision/recall or AUC offline; retained revenue from interventions online Nail those four and the modeling almost chooses itself. Get them wrong and the fanciest model is solving the wrong problem. Note that accuracy is misleading for rare events — churn is rare, so nobody churns scores high and is useless — so always separate the offline ML metric from the online business metric you ll A/B test. Memory hook To crispen any vague ML ask, answer I-O-L-M: Input (known at prediction time?), Output (what exactly, with what horizon?), Label (where s the ground truth?), Metric (success tied to business value?). Interview angle For any how would you build X with ML? question, spend your first 90 seconds on framing — input, precise output with horizon, label source, business-tied metric — then mention a baseline, then talk models. Candidates who jump straight to I d use XGBoost signal they ve never owned a problem end to end. Rapid fire — Workflow amp; framing Lifecycle: Frame → Data → Baseline → Iterate → Evaluate → Deploy/monitor. Most time goes to Data. Always build a dumb baseline first: it calibrates expectations and surfaces leakage. Iterate on validation; touch the test set once at Evaluate. Deployment isn t the end: monitor for drift and plan retraining. Crispen any vague problem with I-O-L-M, tied to business value. Separate the offline ML metric from the online business metric. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember What ML is Inferring rules from examples; the real goal is generalization , not training fit. title: Generalization
text: Say it in 30s: A model generalizes if it performs well on data it never saw during training. The whole point of ML is low error on the true distribution, not low error on the training set. Held-out data is how we estimate it. Key points The i.i.d. assumption is the license to even hope for generalization: test data is statistically like training data. Train / validation / test split : train fits parameters, validation tunes hyperparameters and model choice, test is touched once for an unbiased final estimate. Distribution shift is the #1 reason good offline models disappoint in production — the i.i.d. assumption quietly fails. The generalization gap = test error − training error; large gap signals overfitting. Trap: any decision made by looking at the test set leaks information and inflates your estimate. Guard the test set. See depth: Fundamentals (§3). Related: Empirical Risk Minimization , Overfitting Underfitting , Cross-Validation , Bias-Variance Tradeoff .

title: Overfitting & Underfitting
text: Say it in 30s: Underfitting = the model is too simple to capture the signal (high training error AND high test error). Overfitting = the model memorizes the training sample including its noise (low training error, high test error). You diagnose which one you have from the gap between training and validation curves. Reading the learning curve Big gap that doesn t close with more data → high variance / overfitting → more data, regularization, simpler model. Both curves plateau high and sit close together → high bias / underfitting → richer model or better features (more data won t help). Fixes Overfitting: regularization, dropout, early stopping, data augmentation, more data, ensembling. Underfitting: more capacity, better/more features, train longer, reduce regularization. Trap: a low training error alone tells you nothing. Always quote the validation gap. See depth: Fundamentals (§3–4). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Regularization , Cross-Validation , Generalization .

title: Regularization
text: Say it in 30s: Anything that constrains a model to reduce variance at the cost of a little bias. Most often an added penalty on model complexity: minimize (empirical loss + λ·penalty). λ trades fit against simplicity. L1 vs L2 (the classic question) L2 / Ridge (penalize Σwᵢ²): shrinks weights smoothly toward zero, never exactly zero. Handles correlated features by sharing weight. Has a closed form. L1 / Lasso (penalize Σ|wᵢ|): drives some weights exactly to zero → built-in feature selection / sparsity. The corner of the diamond constraint is why. No closed form (subgradient / soft-thresholding at zero). Elastic Net : L1 + L2, gets sparsity plus stability with correlated features. Beyond penalties: early stopping, dropout, data augmentation, weight decay, ensembling are all variance-fighting regularizers. Trap: larger λ = more regularization = more bias, less variance. Tune λ on validation, not test. See depth: Loss Functions (§2.5–2.6), Regression Methods (§3.3), Fundamentals (§5). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Overfitting Underfitting .

title: Gradient Descent
text: Say it in 30s: An iterative optimizer. Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters, then step in the negative gradient direction. Repeat. The learning rate sets the step size. It converges to a stationary point of differentiable losses (the global minimum if the loss is convex) without solving for it in closed form. Variants Batch GD : gradient over the whole dataset each step — stable, slow, memory-heavy. SGD : one example (or mini-batch) at a time — noisy but fast, and the noise can help escape sharp minima. Mini-batch SGD : the practical default. Momentum / Adam / RMSProp : adapt the step using past gradients to go faster and handle ill-conditioning. The one update step: w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w . For linear regression with MSE, ∂L/∂w = (2/n) Xᵀ(Xw − y) . Traps Learning rate too high → diverge; too low → crawl. Non-convex losses (neural nets) → only convergence to a stationary point (often a saddle or plateau), not a global minimum; that s usually fine in practice. Always scale/standardize features so the loss surface isn t a stretched ravine. See depth: Math (§5), TensorGym Study Notes . title: Math
heads: Linear algebra — the words for data
Statistics — from data back to the model
The bootstrap — uncertainty without a formula
Information theory — where loss functions come from
text: Four languages — linear algebra, probability, statistics, optimization — plus information theory, where loss functions secretly come from. After this chapter you can Read any model as matrix operations on data; state Bayes rule and explain MLE vs MAP; say what a p-value and a confidence interval actually mean; explain why gradient descent works and when it doesn t; and derive cross-entropy from first principles. # Linear algebra — the words for data Almost every model is linear algebra with a nonlinearity sprinkled on top. A dataset is a matrix X X X of shape n × d n \times d n × d : n n n rows (examples) by d d d columns (features). A single example is a vector; a batch is a matrix; an image or a sequence of embeddings is a tensor. Once you see data as a matrix, a linear layer is just W x + b Wx + b W x + b — a matrix multiply that maps one vector space into another. Object Shape What it is Scalar 1 1 1 A single number (a learning rate, a loss value) Vector d d d One example, one feature column, one embedding Matrix m × n m \times n m × n A dataset ( n × d n \times d n × d ), a weight layer, a covariance ( d × d d \times d d × d ) Tensor 3D+ A batch of images, a sequence of token embeddings Two operations carry most of the weight. The dot product a ⋅ b a \cdot b a ⋅ b measures alignment: large when two vectors point the same way, zero when orthogonal. Normalize it and you get cosine similarity — the backbone of search, embeddings, and attention. Matrix–vector multiplication W x Wx W x is a linear transformation that rotates, scales, and projects the input; stacking these with nonlinearities is the entire forward pass of a neural net. Norms measure size. The L2 norm ∥ w ∥ 2 \lVert w \rVert_2 ∥ w ∥ 2 ​ is Euclidean length and underlies ridge regression; the L1 norm ∥ w ∥ 1 \lVert w \rVert_1 ∥ w ∥ 1 ​ sums absolute values and drives sparsity (lasso). The choice of norm decides whether your regularizer shrinks weights smoothly or zeroes them out. The two ideas interviewers probe are eigendecomposition and SVD . An eigenvector is a direction a transformation only stretches, never rotates. The eigenvectors of a covariance matrix are the axes of greatest variance — which is exactly PCA . The singular value decomposition A = U Σ V ⊤ A = U\Sigma V^\top A = U Σ V ⊤ factors any matrix into rotate–scale–rotate, and powers PCA, low-rank approximation, recommender systems, and pseudo-inverses. Understand SVD and half of classical ML stops looking like separate tricks. PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance; keep the top-k for the best linear summary. Interview cue Why does PCA use eigenvectors of the covariance matrix? Because they are the orthogonal directions that maximize retained variance; the eigenvalues say how much each captures, so the top-k give the best rank-k linear summary of the data. # Eigen-everything: directions that don t rotate Most vectors are knocked off course by a matrix transformation, but a few stay perfectly aligned. An eigenvector is a special direction that a square matrix A A A only scales, never rotates. The scaling factor is the eigenvalue λ \lambda λ . Formally, A v = λ v Av = \lambda v A v = λ v . Take A = [ 2 1 1 2 ] A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 1 \\ 1 2 \end{bmatrix} A = [ 2 1 ​ 1 2 ​ ] . Solving the characteristic equation det ⁡ ( A − λ I ) = 0 \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 det ( A − λ I ) = 0 yields roots at λ 1 = 3 \lambda_1 = 3 λ 1 ​ = 3 and λ 2 = 1 \lambda_2 = 1 λ 2 ​ = 1 . The corresponding unit eigenvectors are v 1 = [ 1 2 , 1 2 ] ⊤ v_1 = [\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}]^\top v 1 ​ = [ 2 ​ 1 ​ , 2 ​ 1 ​ ] ⊤ and v 2 = [ 1 2 , − 1 2 ] ⊤ v_2 = [\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}]^\top v 2 ​ = [ 2 ​ 1 ​ , − 2 ​ 1 ​ ] ⊤ . Notice that A v 1 = [ 3 , 3 ] ⊤ Av_1 = [3, 3]^\top A v 1 ​ = [ 3 , 3 ] ⊤ — the vector is simply stretched by a factor of 3 along its original axis. The eigenvector defines the space s orientation, while the eigenvalue measures the magnitude of variance or spread along that specific axis. # Probability — measuring uncertainty Probability is the language for everything a model doesn t know. A random variable takes values with a distribution: a pmf for discrete outcomes, a pdf for continuous ones (where probability lives in areas, not points). A few distributions show up constantly: Distribution Models Shows up as Bernoulli / Binomial One / many yes-no trials Binary labels, click/no-click Categorical / Multinomial One-of-k outcomes Softmax outputs, class labels Gaussian (Normal) Sums of many small effects Noise, weight init, CLT Poisson / Exponential Counts / waiting times Arrivals, rare events, survival Uniform No prior preference Initialization, sampling From a distribution you get expectation (mean), variance (spread), and covariance (co-movement). Learn to move between the joint p ( x , y ) p(x, y) p ( x , y ) , the marginal p ( x ) = ∑ y p ( x , y ) p(x) = \sum_y p(x, y) p ( x ) = ∑ y ​ p ( x , y ) , and the conditional p ( y ∣ x ) = p ( x , y ) / p ( x ) p(y \mid x) = p(x, y) / p(x) p ( y ∣ x ) = p ( x , y ) / p ( x ) . Independence means p ( x , y ) = p ( x ) p ( y ) p(x, y) = p(x)\,p(y) p ( x , y ) = p ( x ) p ( y ) — knowing one tells you nothing about the other. The single most important formula in the chapter is Bayes rule : p ( θ ∣ data ) = p ( data ∣ θ ) p ( θ ) p ( data ) ⟹ posterior ∝ likelihood × prior p(\theta \mid \text{data}) = \frac{p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}{p(\text{data})} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \text{posterior} \propto \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior} p ( θ ∣ data ) = p ( data ) p ( data ∣ θ ) p ( θ ) ​ ⟹ posterior ∝ likelihood × prior The prior belief, reshaped by the likelihood of the data, yields the posterior. Two estimation principles fall out of it. Maximum Likelihood (MLE) picks the θ \theta θ that makes the observed data most probable — ignoring the prior. Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) maximizes the posterior — MLE plus a prior, and that prior term is exactly regularization (a Gaussian prior gives L2, a Laplace prior gives L1). This is the bridge between probability and the losses you minimize. Interview cue — the base-rate trap A test is 99% accurate for a disease affecting 1 in 10,000. You test positive — the chance you have it is roughly 1%, not 99%, because the tiny prior is swamped by false positives. Reaching for Bayes instead of the headline number is the signal. # Statistics — from data back to the model Probability reasons from a known model to data; statistics runs it backwards — from a finite sample to claims about the population. An estimator is any rule computed from data (the sample mean estimates the true mean). Estimators have their own bias and variance: unbiased means right on average, and the standard error is how much it wobbles from sample to sample. The reason any of this works is the Central Limit Theorem : the distribution of a sample mean approaches a Gaussian as n n n grows, whatever the population looks like. That s what lets us attach error bars without knowing the true distribution. Even a skewed population produces a near-Gaussian distribution of the sample mean. A confidence interval is a procedure that traps the true value 95% of the time over repeated sampling — not 95% probability the truth is in this particular interval. Hypothesis testing assumes a null (no effect) and asks how surprising the data would be under it; that surprise is the p-value : P ( result at least this extreme ∣ null true ) P(\text{result at least this extreme} \mid \text{null true}) P ( result at least this extreme ∣ null true ) . It is not the probability the null is true, and not the false-positive rate. A Type I error is a false alarm, a Type II error is a miss, and power is the chance of catching a real effect. Two traps: correlation is not causation (a confounder can drive both), and Simpson s paradox (a within-group trend can reverse when pooled). The thread to ML: MLE is the statistical backbone of training — squared error is MLE under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is MLE for a categorical model. Interview cue What does a p-value mean? is the most failed stats question. Say: P ( data this extreme ∣ null true ) P(\text{data this extreme} \mid \text{null true}) P ( data this extreme ∣ null true ) . A small p-value means the data is surprising under the null — evidence against it, nothing more. # The bootstrap — uncertainty without a formula Sometimes you need the uncertainty of an estimator with no clean formula. The bootstrap treats your sample as a stand-in for the population, then resamples from it with replacement many times, recomputing the statistic each time. The spread of those values approximates the true sampling distribution — standard errors and intervals by brute force instead of algebra. It works because a large sample resembles the population. Each bootstrap sample contains about 63.2% of the distinct original points, leaving ~36.8% out-of-bag — a free held-out set. This is the basis of bagging and random forests: each tree trains on a resampled dataset, averaging cuts variance, and out-of-bag points give a built-in validation estimate. # Optimization — how models actually learn Training is optimization: define a loss, then search for parameters that make it small. The workhorse is gradient descent — compute the gradient (steepest increase) and step the opposite way: w ← w − η ∇ w L w \leftarrow w - \eta\, \nabla_w L w ← w − η ∇ w ​ L . The learning rate η \eta η sets the step size: too large overshoots or diverges, too small crawls. The learning rate is the whole game: the right size converges, too large diverges. Variant Uses per step Trade-off Batch GD All data Stable, accurate; slow, memory-heavy Stochastic (SGD) One example Fast, noisy; noise escapes bad minima Mini-batch A small batch The default — GPU-efficient, stable enough Plain SGD is slow on ravine-shaped losses, so modern optimizers add memory. Momentum accumulates velocity to power through flat regions; RMSProp scales each parameter s step by its recent gradient magnitude; Adam combines both and is the deep-net default. A convex loss has one global bowl (linear/logistic regression, SVMs); deep nets are non-convex, but the real obstacle is usually saddle points and plateaus, not bad local minima — exactly what momentum and adaptive methods escape. Interview cue Why mini-batch SGD? It fits in memory, updates far more often per epoch, and its gradient noise mildly regularizes. Why Adam? Per-parameter adaptive steps plus momentum make it robust to learning-rate choice and fast to converge. # Information theory — where loss functions come from Information theory answers how surprising is an outcome, and how many bits to encode it? Entropy is a distribution s average surprise — high when outcomes are unpredictable, low when one dominates. Cross-entropy H ( p , q ) H(p, q) H ( p , q ) is the average bits to encode data from the true p p p using a model q q q . KL divergence is the gap D K L ( p ∥ q ) = H ( p , q ) − H ( p ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \Vert q) = H(p, q) - H(p) D KL ​ ( p ∥ q ) = H ( p , q ) − H ( p ) : how much worse your model is than the truth, zero only when q = p q = p q = p . This is why cross-entropy is the classification loss , not an arbitrary choice. Minimizing cross-entropy between true labels and predicted probabilities equals minimizing KL divergence to the true distribution, which equals maximum likelihood for a categorical model — three framings, one objective. Squared error is the same story under a Gaussian assumption. Mutual information — how much one variable reduces uncertainty about another — rounds out the toolkit. Interview cue Why cross-entropy and not MSE for classification? Cross-entropy is the MLE/KL-minimizing loss for probabilities, and its gradient stays strong when the model is confidently wrong; MSE s gradient vanishes there (via the sigmoid), so it learns slowly and is non-convex for logistic models. # One-page summary Topic The one thing to remember Linear algebra Data is a matrix; models are matrix multiplies. Dot product = similarity; SVD/eigen = PCA, low-rank, recommenders. Norms L2 shrinks smoothly (ridge); L1 zeroes out (lasso). Probability Move fluently between joint, marginal, conditional. Bayes: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. MLE vs MAP MLE = fit data; MAP = MLE + prior, and the prior is regularization (Gaussian→L2, Laplace→L1). Statistics Sample → population. CLT makes the sample mean Gaussian. A CI is a procedure, not a probability about one interval. p-value P ( data this extreme ∣ null true ) P(\text{data this extreme} \mid \text{null true}) P ( data this extreme ∣ null true ) . Not P(null true), not the false-positive rate. Bootstrap Resample with replacement for uncertainty without a formula; ~63% in-bag. Basis of bagging. Optimization Gradient descent; mini-batch is the default; Adam = momentum + adaptive steps. Saddle points are the real enemy. Information theory Cross-entropy = KL-to-truth = MLE for classification. Squared error = MLE under Gaussian noise. # Related Gradient Descent Maximum Likelihood Estimation Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD

title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text: Say it in 30s: Pick the parameters that make the observed data most probable. Maximize the likelihood (equivalently, minimize negative log-likelihood). Most common losses are NLL in disguise: the assumed noise model determines the loss. The key insight interviewers want Assume Gaussian noise on a regression target → MLE gives MSE / least squares . Assume Bernoulli/categorical labels → MLE gives cross-entropy / log loss . So every loss is a hidden assumption about the noise — the loss is not arbitrary. MLE vs MAP MLE maximizes P(data | θ). MAP maximizes P(θ | data) ∝ P(data | θ)·P(θ) — adding a prior. A Gaussian prior on weights = L2 regularization ; a Laplace prior = L1 . Trap: MLE can overfit with little data (no prior); that s exactly why regularization (= a prior) helps. See depth: Loss Functions (§2.1), Math (§6). Related: Cross-Entropy Loss , Regularization , Empirical Risk Minimization .

title: Cross-Entropy Loss
text: Say it in 30s: The standard loss for classification. It measures the distance between the true label distribution and the predicted probability distribution. For a true class, it s −log(predicted probability of that class) — you re penalized by how surprised the model was about the right answer. Why it beats MSE for classification It pairs with softmax/sigmoid to give a well-behaved loss (convex in the logits, and in the weights for a linear model such as logistic regression) with strong gradients even when the model is confidently wrong (MSE s gradient vanishes there → slow learning). It s the maximum-likelihood loss under a Bernoulli/categorical model, so it s the principled choice. Forms Binary: −[y·log p + (1−y)·log(1−p)] , paired with sigmoid . Multiclass: −Σ yᵢ log pᵢ , paired with softmax . Traps Feed logits to the loss (e.g. CrossEntropyLoss in PyTorch already applies softmax) — don t softmax twice. Numerically unstable if you compute log(softmax) naively; use log-sum-exp / built-in fused versions. See depth: Loss Functions (§2.3–2.4), TensorGym Study Notes . Related: Maximum Likelihood Estimation , Logistic Regression , Gradient Descent .

A loss function is the scorecard in golf. Every swing (prediction) gets a number for how far you landed from the hole (the truth). You don t need the scorecard to play — you need it to improve . title: ML System Design Framework
text: The repeatable spine for any ML system design prompt. The strongest answers spend the first third scoping and never jump straight to a model. Drive this structure yourself — don t wait to be asked. # The 6 steps # 1. Clarify frame (~5 min) Turn the vague prompt into a concrete ML problem. Pin down: Business goal and who the user is Scale — DAU, # items, QPS Latency budget (e.g. ~100ms for ranking) Freshness requirements What good actually means Open with: First I ll align on the goal and success metric, then scale and latency, then ask what data we have. # 2. ML task metrics What does the model predict ? Framing: ranking vs classification vs retrieval. Offline metrics (AUC, NDCG, recall@k) AND online metrics (CTR, watch time, revenue) AND guardrails. The key move: the proxy you optimize ≠ the thing you actually care about. Tune proxy weights against an online north-star (e.g. D7/D30 retention) via A/B tests. # 3. Data features Sources, labels (explicit vs implicit), leakage, cold start. Feature families: user · item · user×item cross · context. The cross features are where ranking earns its keep. Implicit-feedback bias — name all three: Exposure / selection bias (feedback loop — you only see labels for what you showed) Position bias (rank drives clicks regardless of quality) Noisy negatives (a skip ≠ a confirmed dislike) Fixes: negative sampling, inverse propensity weighting / position-as-feature (zeroed at serving), exploration traffic to break the loop. # 4. Model Start with a baseline , then justify complexity. For large scale: multistage — retrieval → ranking → re-ranking. Discuss tradeoffs , not just the fanciest option. # 5. Serving scale Retrieval: two-tower model + ANN index (HNSW / ScaNN / FAISS). Item embeddings precomputed offline indexed; user tower runs once per request → single ANN lookup. The decoupling is the serving win. Multiple retrieval sources unioned (personalized + trending + social + fresh-exploration). Feature store, online vs batch inference, caching. # 6. Evaluation iteration Offline: ranking metric (NDCG), check calibration if probs feed downstream. Online: A/B test vs north-star (retention) + guardrail metrics (reports, diversity, creator health). Post-launch: monitor feature prediction drift , watch online metrics decay, retrain regularly (daily/continuous for fast domains). Continuous retraining on biased logs amplifies bias → exploration matters long-term. # Two-stage architecture cheat Stage Catalog → out Job Model Retrieval billions → thousands recall, cheap two-tower + ANN Ranking thousands → hundreds precision heavy multi-task (MMoE) Re-rank hundreds → ~10 diversity, policy rules + light model # Cold start Item: content embeddings at upload → retrievable immediately (also = freshness story). User: onboarding preferences + popular/trending prior, let real interactions take over. # Common ways people fail Jump straight to the model. Never define metrics properly (or don t connect offline ↔ online). Ignore data/serving reality. Circle instead of committing — state the structured answer up front. Use generic language instead of canonical component names. MOC - System Design · Home
