text: Prompt: Design a system that predicts whether a user will click on a given ad, powering the ad auction and ranking for a large social media platform. ~2B DAU, ~10M active ad campaigns, billions of impression decisions daily. See the spine: ML System Design Framework . # What I covered Objective — eventually got to advertiser revenue, but took multiple prompts. Did not arrive at bid × pCTR × pCVR or eCPM on my own. Retrieval — correctly proposed two-tower with ANN lookup; understood decoupled serving (precompute ad embeddings offline, compute user embedding at inference). Ranking — identified that a richer model is needed post-retrieval but could not name the architecture (DCN, Wide Deep, DeepFM). Went blank. Re-ranking — mentioned diversity and business rules; mentioned position bias unprompted. Training data — described features instead of labels when asked. Did not surface downsampling/recalibration, delayed conversions, or selection bias (ESMM). Serving — could not describe the inference flow, feature store tiers, or latency budget breakdown. Monitoring — mentioned drift but initially confused predicted CTR dropping with model degradation. Did not mention calibration ratio or NE. Guardrails — did not volunteer click fraud, legal targeting constraints, or budget pacing. # Key concepts taught during mock # Business objective Revenue = Σ (bid × pCTR × pCVR) for CPA bids (CPC: bid × pCTR; CPM: bid); ranking by eCPM per bid type GSP/VCG-style auction (second-price in the single-slot case); normalize CPC/CPM/CPA into common currency Calibration matters because probabilities directly feed auction pricing # Ranking model (pCTR / pCVR) Industry standard: Deep Cross Network (DCN) or Wide Deep Why: explicit feature crosses are king in CTR prediction (user segment × ad category × context) Evolution: logistic regression → GBDT → Wide Deep → DeepFM → DCN Key difference from retrieval: can now use cross-features (user-ad interaction features) # Position bias Ads higher in feed get more clicks regardless of relevance Fix: train with position as feature, drop at inference Shallow tower (Google/YouTube) or PAL (Huawei) # Training data gotchas Labels: click=1/no-click=0 for pCTR; conversion=1/no-conversion=0 for pCVR Class imbalance: CTR ~1-3%. Use negative downsampling + recalibrate: p_true = p_sampled / (p_sampled + (1-p_sampled)/sampling_rate) Delayed conversions: tension between freshness and completeness of conversion labels Selection bias in pCVR: only observe conversions on clicked ads; ESMM (Alibaba) trains pCVR on all impressions # Serving architecture Offline features: user profiles, historical aggregates, ad embeddings → feature store (Redis/KV), sub-ms lookup Near-real-time features: streaming via Kafka + Flink, e.g., user impressions last hour → seconds-stale Real-time features: computed at request time (position, time, context) Flow: request → retrieval (ANN, 10ms) → feature assembly (batch KV lookup, 5-10ms) → ranking inference (10-20ms) → auction + business rules (5ms) → total ~50ms Prediction service (TF Serving / Triton) separate from feature store # Ads-specific concerns (should volunteer) Click fraud: bots/competitors draining budgets; need fraud detection layer Feedback loops: model predictions affect training data distribution Fairness/legal: housing, employment, credit ads cannot target by protected attributes Budget pacing: smooth advertiser spend across the day, don t exhaust budget early # Monitoring Calibration ratio (predicted/observed CTR) sliced by advertiser, category, segment Normalized cross-entropy (NE) — better than AUC because it measures calibration, not just ranking Revenue metrics: RPM, eCPM Auction health: unexpected shifts in winning bids # Gaps to close before next mock DCN / Wide Deep architecture — read the Google papers, know the diagram Feature serving tiers and latency budgets Training data: downsampling + calibration formula, delayed conversions, ESMM Proactively volunteer: click fraud, pacing, legal constraints, monitoring Commit to specifics faster — don t circle on business objective

title: Time Series Stationarity
heads: The four components of a series
ACF and PACF — reading the order of a model
text: Time-series forecasting — the one corner of ML where the i.i.d. assumption is dead on arrival: order is the signal, and the past leaks into the future. After this chapter You can say why time series breaks ordinary ML; decompose a series and test it for stationarity; read ACF/PACF to pick model orders; write down the AR, MA, ARIMA, and exponential-smoothing equations; choose between classical and ML approaches; and validate with the right backtest and metric. # Why time series is different In standard supervised learning the examples are exchangeable — shuffle the rows and nothing changes. A time series is the opposite: each observation y t y_t y t ​ is indexed by time, and order is the signal . Observations are autocorrelated ( y t y_t y t ​ depends on its own past), so you can never shuffle or do random train/test splits — doing so trains on the future to predict the past, the most fatal leak in forecasting. And the process itself often changes over time, so the distribution is moving. The mindset: a forecast is a conditional expectation y ^ t + h = E [ y t + h ∣ information up to t ] \hat{y}_{t+h} = \mathbb{E}[y_{t+h} \mid \text{information up to } t] y ^ ​ t + h ​ = E [ y t + h ​ ∣ information up to t ] . # The four components of a series The classical lens decomposes a series into four parts; most models target one explicitly. Additive decomposition: the observed series is the sum of trend, seasonal, and residual parts. Component What it is Example Trend ( T T T ) Long-run direction A product s user base growing over years Seasonality ( S S S ) Fixed, known-period cycle Retail spiking every December; traffic by hour Cyclical ( C C C ) Long swings, no fixed period Business cycles — harder to model Residual ( R R R ) What s left after structure Irregular, ideally unpredictable The distinction interviewers like: seasonality has a fixed period (12 months, 7 days) while a cycle does not — that s why seasonality is easy to encode and cycles are not. # Additive vs multiplicative How the components combine is a modeling choice. The additive model assumes they add: y t = T t + S t + R t y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t y t ​ = T t ​ + S t ​ + R t ​ Use it when the seasonal swing is a roughly constant size regardless of level. The multiplicative model assumes they multiply: y t = T t × S t × R t y_t = T_t \times S_t \times R_t y t ​ = T t ​ × S t ​ × R t ​ Use it when the swing scales with the level (December is always +30%). A key trick: logs turn multiplicative into additive, since log ⁡ ( T ⋅ S ⋅ R ) = log ⁡ T + log ⁡ S + log ⁡ R \log(T\cdot S\cdot R) = \log T + \log S + \log R lo g ( T ⋅ S ⋅ R ) = lo g T + lo g S + lo g R — which is why log-transforming is the standard first move when variance grows with the level. # Stationarity Most classical models assume the series is stationary : statistical properties don t change over time. Weak (covariance) stationarity requires a constant mean, constant variance, and an autocovariance Cov ⁡ ( y t , y t + k ) \operatorname{Cov}(y_t, y_{t+k}) Cov ( y t ​ , y t + k ​ ) that depends only on the lag k k k , not absolute time. A stationary series has stable structure, so a fixed set of coefficients can capture it. Differencing turns a trending (non-stationary) series into one with a stable mean. The usual fix is differencing — model the change, ∇ y t = y t − y t − 1 \nabla y_t = y_t - y_{t-1} ∇ y t ​ = y t ​ − y t − 1 ​ — which removes a linear trend; seasonal differencing y t − y t − m y_t - y_{t-m} y t ​ − y t − m ​ removes a season of length m m m . The number of differences needed is the d d d in ARIMA. Confirm with a unit-root test (Augmented Dickey–Fuller), whose null is non-stationary ; a small p-value means you can treat it as stationary. Use the minimum d d d — over-differencing injects artificial autocorrelation. # ACF and PACF — reading the order of a model Two plots tell you which classical model to use. The ACF at lag k k k is the correlation between y t y_t y t ​ and y t − k y_{t-k} y t − k ​ , including indirect effects through intermediate lags. The PACF at lag k k k is the same correlation after removing all shorter lags — the direct effect only. AR(2) signature: the PACF cuts off at the AR order while the ACF decays. MA is the mirror image. Plot pattern Implies PACF cuts off after lag p p p ; ACF tails off AR( p p p ) — read p p p from the PACF ACF cuts off after lag q q q ; PACF tails off MA( q q q ) — read q q q from the ACF Both tail off gradually ARMA( p , q p, q p , q ) — pick via AIC/BIC # Classical models: the ARIMA family ARIMA is built from two atoms. An autoregressive AR( p p p ) model says today is a linear function of its own recent past plus noise: y t = c + ϕ 1 y t − 1 + ϕ 2 y t − 2 + ⋯ + ϕ p y t − p + ε t y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \dots + \phi_p y_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t y t ​ = c + ϕ 1 ​ y t − 1 ​ + ϕ 2 ​ y t − 2 ​ + ⋯ + ϕ p ​ y t − p ​ + ε t ​ A moving-average MA( q q q ) model says today is a function of recent shocks (past forecast errors): y t = μ + ε t + θ 1 ε t − 1 + θ 2 ε t − 2 + ⋯ + θ q ε t − q y_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1 \varepsilon_{t-1} + \theta_2 \varepsilon_{t-2} + \dots + \theta_q \varepsilon_{t-q} y t ​ = μ + ε t ​ + θ 1 ​ ε t − 1 ​ + θ 2 ​ ε t − 2 ​ + ⋯ + θ q ​ ε t − q ​ Combine them for ARMA( p , q p, q p , q ) ; apply it to a series differenced d d d times and you get ARIMA( p , d , q p, d, q p , d , q ) — difference until stationary, then explain it with p p p autoregressive and q q q moving-average terms. SARIMA adds a seasonal set of terms at lag m m m ; ARIMAX/SARIMAX add exogenous regressors (promotions, holidays, price). Orders come from ACF/PACF plus minimizing AIC/BIC; auto_arima automates the search. Interview cue Difference between AR and MA? AR regresses on past observed values; MA regresses on past errors/shocks. AR has long memory (a shock propagates through the recursion); a pure MA( q q q ) remembers exactly q q q steps. # Exponential smoothing (ETS) The other classical family forecasts with a weighted average of past observations whose weights decay exponentially — recent data matters most. Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES) tracks just the level: ℓ t = α y t + ( 1 − α ) ℓ t − 1 , y ^ t + h = ℓ t \ell_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1 - \alpha)\,\ell_{t-1}, \qquad \hat{y}_{t+h} = \ell_t ℓ t ​ = α y t ​ + ( 1 − α ) ℓ t − 1 ​ , y ^ ​ t + h ​ = ℓ t ​ α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \alpha \in (0,1] α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] sets how fast old data is forgotten. SES has no trend or seasonality, so it forecasts a flat line. Holt adds a trend equation (sloped forecast); Holt–Winters adds a seasonal one. Modern libraries frame these as the ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonal) state-space family with likelihood fitting and prediction intervals. Useful fact: SES ≡ \equiv ≡ ARIMA(0,1,1) and Holt ≡ \equiv ≡ ARIMA(0,2,2) — two languages for an overlapping set of processes. Model Captures Forecast shape SES Level only Flat Holt Level + trend Sloped line Holt–Winters Level + trend + seasonality Sloped line with repeating season # Modern / ML approaches With many related series, long histories, rich covariates, or nonlinearities, ML methods take over. Approach Idea Shines when Lags + gradient boosting Engineer lag/rolling/calendar features, fit XGBoost/LightGBM Tabular forecasting with strong covariates Prophet Trend + Fourier seasonality + holidays, fit Bayesian Business series, holidays, gaps; interpretable DeepAR Autoregressive RNN across many series, outputs a distribution Thousands of related series; needs uncertainty N-BEATS / N-HiTS Deep fully-connected basis expansion, no recurrence Strong pure-DL univariate accuracy Temporal Fusion Transformer Attention over mixed covariates; quantiles Multi-horizon with mixed covariate types Two ideas matter more than any architecture. The shift from local models (one ARIMA per series) to global models (one network across all series) lets a sparse series borrow strength from similar ones — a main reason global models (e.g. LightGBM in M5, the ES-RNN hybrid in M4) won recent M-competitions. And probabilistic forecasting — outputting quantiles or a full distribution — matters because inventory and staffing decisions live in the tails. Note that well-tuned classical models and gradient boosting remain hard to beat on a single short series; deep learning earns its keep at scale. # Validation done right You cannot use random K-fold — it leaks the future. The correct procedure respects time: train up to time t t t , forecast the next h h h steps, score, then roll the cutoff forward and repeat. Time-series cross-validation: train on the past, test on the next block, roll forward. An expanding window keeps all history; a sliding window keeps a fixed recent window (better under drift). Three details separate a correct backtest from a broken one: forecast at the same horizon h h h you care about in production; insert a gap if features look ahead; and build every feature from information available at prediction time. Always compare against a naive baseline ( tomorrow = today, this December = last December ) — a model that can t beat the last value isn t worth shipping. # Forecasting metrics Metric Idea Watch out for MAE mean ∣ y − y ^ ∣ \text{mean}\,\lvert y - \hat{y}\rvert mean ∣ y − y ^ ​ ∣ Robust; same units; linear in error RMSE mean ( y − y ^ ) 2 \sqrt{\text{mean}\,(y - \hat{y})^2} mean ( y − y ^ ​ ) 2 ​ Penalizes big misses; outlier-sensitive MAPE mean ∣ y − y ^ ∣ / ∣ y ∣ \text{mean}\,\lvert y - \hat{y}\rvert / \lvert y\rvert mean ∣ y − y ^ ​ ∣ / ∣ y ∣ Explodes near zero; asymmetric MASE MAE ÷ naive model’s MAE \text{MAE} \div \text{naive model s MAE} MAE ÷ naive model’s MAE Cleanest: 1 1 1 beats naive; scale-free WAPE ∑ ∣ y − y ^ ∣ / ∑ ∣ y ∣ \sum\lvert y - \hat{y}\rvert / \sum\lvert y\rvert ∑ ∣ y − y ^ ​ ∣ / ∑ ∣ y ∣ Volume-weighted; popular in retail Pinball loss asymmetric per-quantile loss For probabilistic forecasts; pair with coverage Choose by the decision: RMSE when big misses are costly, MAE/WAPE when cost is linear, MASE for scale-free comparison across series, and pinball loss + coverage for distributions. Avoid MAPE for series that approach zero. Interview cue Why not MAPE? Undefined at zero, blows up for small actuals, and asymmetric — so it quietly rewards under-forecasting. Reach for MASE (scale-free, naive-anchored) or WAPE. # One-page summary Topic The one thing to remember Why it s different Order is the signal; data is autocorrelated; never shuffle or random-split. Components Trend + seasonality (fixed period) + cycle (no fixed period) + noise (in practice the cycle is folded into trend or residual). Additive vs multiplicative Constant swing → additive; swing scales with level → multiplicative (log makes it additive). Stationarity Constant mean/variance/autocovariance. Difference to remove trend; ADF to confirm; minimum d d d . ACF / PACF PACF cuts at p p p → AR( p p p ); ACF cuts at q q q → MA( q q q ); both tail → ARMA. ARIMA family AR = past values; MA = past errors; I = differencing. SARIMA adds seasonality; X adds covariates. Exponential smoothing Exponentially decaying weights. SES (level) → Holt (+trend) → Holt–Winters (+season). Modern ML Lags + boosting; Prophet; DeepAR/TFT/N-BEATS. Global local at scale; forecast distributions. Validation Rolling/expanding backtest at the production horizon; beat a naive baseline. Metrics RMSE (big misses), MAE/WAPE (linear), MASE (scale-free), pinball+coverage (probabilistic). Avoid MAPE near zero. # Related Cross-Validation

title: ML System Design Interview Prep
text: # Stage 1: Business Objective Goal: Understand WHY this system exists before touching anything technical. Interviewers want to see you think before building. Questions to ask: What is the core business goal? (revenue, safety, engagement, retention?) What is the scale? (DAU, QPS, catalog size) What latency is acceptable? ( 100ms real-time, 1s near-real-time, batch OK?) What data freshness is needed? (model needs to reflect events from 5 min ago or 5 days ago?) Are there hard constraints? (regulatory, fairness, GDPR, COPPA, geographic) Which is worse: false positives or false negatives? Is there an existing system? What s broken about it? Business metrics to know: CTR, CVR (conversion rate), GMV DAU/MAU, retention, session length Map FP/FN cost to business: fraud FN = money lost, fraud FP = user friction # Stage 2: ML Objective Goal: Translate business goal → concrete ML problem. Task types: Binary classification — spam, fraud, click prediction Multi-class — intent detection, category tagging Ranking / LTR — search, feed, recommendations Regression — price, ETA, bid value Multi-task — predict CTR + CVR jointly Generative — query rewriting, summarization Business metric → ML proxy: Business Metric ML Proxy CTR AUC-ROC, log loss Revenue CVR, predicted value Relevance NDCG, MRR, MAP Safety Recall @ high precision Engagement Predicted watch time Loss functions: Problem Loss Binary classification Binary cross-entropy (log loss) Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy Imbalanced classification Focal loss Regression MSE / MAE / Huber Ranking (pairwise) BPR loss, hinge loss Ranking (listwise) LambdaRank, ApproxNDCG Embeddings / contrastive Triplet loss, NT-Xent (SimCLR) Distillation KL divergence + task loss Key framing decisions: Point-wise vs. pairwise vs. listwise ranking Single-task vs. multi-task (shared bottom, mixture of experts) Do you need calibrated probabilities or just a good ranking? # Stage 3: High-Level Design Goal: Sketch the end-to-end pipeline. Get the boxes and arrows right before going deep. Standard pipeline: Data sources → Feature engineering → Feature store ↓ Training pipeline → Model registry ↓ Serving layer → Prediction store / cache ↓ Logging → Feedback loop Common architecture patterns: Two-tower (retrieval) User tower + Item tower → dot product → ANN index Item embeddings precomputed offline Used by: YouTube, Pinterest, TikTok for candidate generation Cascade / Funnel (retrieval → ranking → re-ranking) Retrieval (ANN, BM25, CF) → Ranking (GBDT, DNN) → Re-ranking (business rules, diversity) Used in: search, feed ranking, ads Sequence model (temporal) LSTM / Transformer over user history → next-item prediction Used in: Netflix, Spotify, TikTok Real-time + batch hybrid Batch features (stable, cheap) + real-time features (fresh, expensive) merged at serving # Stage 4: Data Feature Engineering Goal: Where does data come from, how do you label it, what features do you extract. Data sources: User interaction logs (clicks, watches, purchases, skips, dwell time) Item/entity metadata (title, category, price, content embeddings) Context (time of day, device, location, session position) Social graph (follows, co-views, shares) External signals (weather, trending topics) Labeling strategies: Explicit: ratings, thumbs up/down — sparse, high quality Implicit: clicks, watches, purchases — dense, noisy (click ≠ satisfaction) Proxy labels: watched 50% of video as engagement positive Human annotation: content quality, safety, NLP tasks Label leakage gotchas: Features computed after the event (e.g., final view count when predicting CTR) Future data leaking into training window Feature types: User: demographics, long-term interests, embedding of ID Item: category, price, recency, popularity, content embedding User-item cross: past CTR on this category, historical spend Context: time, device, session position, query Feature engineering techniques: Normalization / standardization — for neural nets Log transform — heavy-tailed distributions (price, counts) Bucketization — continuous → categorical Target encoding — replace category with mean label (watch for leakage) Embeddings — for high-cardinality IDs (users, items, queries) Hashing trick — very high cardinality, reduces memory Feature crosses — jointly encode two features (A × B) Sequence aggregation — mean/sum/attention pooling over user history Feature store: Offline store: Hive, BigQuery, Spark — batch features, used in training Online store: Redis, DynamoDB (managed by Feast / Tecton) — low-latency features at serve time Point-in-time correctness: training features must reflect what was known AT prediction time Class imbalance: Downsample negatives (very common in click prediction — 1:100 or worse) Calibration correction after downsampling negatives at keep-rate w: p = p_s / (p_s + (1-p_s)/w), equivalent to adding log(w) to the logit Weighted loss Focal loss # Stage 5: Model Goal: Choose and justify your model. Know the tradeoffs. Model cheat sheet: Need Model Fast baseline Logistic regression Tabular data, ranking LightGBM / XGBoost Large-scale retrieval Two-tower + FAISS ANN Dense ranking DNN / DCN (Deep Cross Network) Sequential / session Transformer (SASRec, BERT4Rec) Social graph GNN (GraphSAGE, PinSage) Multimodal (text + image) CLIP-style dual encoder Model tradeoffs: Logistic Regression Pros: fast, interpretable, calibrated, easy to debug Cons: low capacity, needs manual feature engineering When: baseline, very high QPS, features already good GBDT (XGBoost, LightGBM) Pros: handles tabular data extremely well, no normalization needed, built-in feature importance Cons: doesn t handle embeddings, hard to do online learning When: ranking, fraud, structured tabular data DNN / MLP Pros: learns feature interactions, handles embeddings end-to-end Cons: more data needed, harder to debug, slower than GBDT When: ranking with many features, multi-task setups Two-Tower Pros: item tower precomputed offline → fast retrieval Cons: no user-item interaction at inference time (shallow) When: retrieval at massive scale Transformer Pros: captures sequential context, state of the art for NLP Cons: expensive to train and serve, needs lots of data When: session modeling, NLP tasks, query understanding GNN Pros: captures social / graph structure natively Cons: complex to build and serve When: social feed ranking, fraud on transaction graphs Training considerations: Learning rate schedule: warmup + cosine decay Regularization: L1/L2, dropout, early stopping Positional bias: items shown first get more clicks — debias during training Exposure bias: model only sees items that were previously shown # Stage 6: Inference Serving Goal: Get predictions to users at scale, efficiently. Batch vs. Real-time vs. Near-real-time: Mode Latency Freshness Use case Batch 0ms (precomputed) Stale (hours/days) Email recs, item embeddings Near-real-time Seconds/minutes Fresh Trending, fraud streaming Real-time 100ms Very fresh Feed ranking, search Serving architectures: Precomputed / lookup: store embeddings or scores in Redis, retrieve at serve time Online inference: feature retrieval → model scoring → post-processing in budget Cascade / multi-stage: cheap model for retrieval → expensive model on small candidate set Latency optimization: Quantization: FP32 → FP16 or INT8 (2-4x speedup, small accuracy loss) Distillation: train small student from large teacher Pruning: remove low-importance weights Caching: cache predictions for popular user/item pairs ANN for retrieval: FAISS, ScaNN, HNSW (millisecond-scale over billions of vectors) Batching: group requests on GPU to maximize throughput Scalability: Horizontal scaling: replica-based, load balanced GPU serving: large batches / transformers CPU serving: low-latency tabular / small models Feature lookup budget: Redis P99 ~1ms, DB can be 10-100ms — budget carefully Deployment strategies: Shadow mode: run new model in parallel, no user impact, compare offline Canary: 1-5% traffic, monitor metrics A/B test: randomized experiment, measure business metric Interleaving: blend two ranked lists, measure clicks — faster signal than A/B Multi-armed bandit: explore/exploit, useful when A/B is too slow # Stage 7: Deep Dives Improvements Goal: Show depth by proactively naming hard problems and how you d solve them. Cold Start New user: popular items, context features (device, referral), demographic priors New item: content embeddings (image, text, metadata), zero-shot via pretrained model Exploration: epsilon-greedy, Thompson sampling, UCB Data Freshness / Training Latency How fast does the model react to new events? Options: real-time feature updates, online learning (SGD on stream), continuous training Tradeoff: freshness vs. stability Model Monitoring Drift Data drift: input distributions shift (COVID changed all user behavior overnight) Concept drift: feature-label relationship changes Detection: KL divergence, PSI (Population Stability Index), shadow scoring Response: automated retraining triggers, alerting Bias Fairness Selection bias: model trained on biased exposure (only seen items) Popularity bias: popular items get over-recommended, feedback loop amplifies Demographic fairness: disparate impact across groups Debiasing: inverse propensity scoring (IPS), adversarial debiasing, constrained optimization Feedback Loops / Echo Chambers Model recommends what it predicts users like → users only see those items → model gets reinforced Mitigations: exploration budgets, diversity constraints, counterfactual evaluation Multi-Objective Optimization Competing objectives: engagement vs. revenue vs. safety vs. diversity Approaches: weighted sum of losses, Pareto optimization, constrained (maximize revenue s.t. engagement ≥ threshold), mixture of experts per objective Reranking After ranking: diversity (no 3 consecutive same artist), freshness boost, sponsored insertion, safety filtering Privacy Differential privacy: calibrated noise on gradients or outputs Federated learning: train on-device, aggregate updates ID hashing = pseudonymization only; not a formal privacy guarantee # Quick Reference Cheat Sheets # Loss Functions Problem Loss Binary classification Binary cross-entropy Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy Imbalanced Focal loss Regression (outlier sensitive) MSE Regression (robust) MAE / Huber Ranking pairwise BPR, hinge Ranking listwise LambdaRank, ApproxNDCG Embeddings Triplet loss, NT-Xent Distillation KL divergence # Models Need Model Baseline Logistic regression Tabular / ranking LightGBM / XGBoost Retrieval at scale Two-tower + FAISS Dense ranking DNN / DCN Session / sequential SASRec / BERT4Rec Graph signals GNN (GraphSAGE, PinSage) Multimodal CLIP-style dual encoder # Inference Need Approach Sub-10ms Precomputed + Redis lookup ~100ms budget Online inference, light model Stale OK Batch + feature store Real-time events Kafka + Flink streaming Large model, throughput matters Quantization + GPU batching Billion-scale retrieval ANN (FAISS, ScaNN, HNSW) # Business Metric → ML Metric Business ML CTR AUC-ROC, log loss Revenue CVR, predicted bid value Relevance NDCG, MRR, MAP Safety Recall @ fixed high precision Engagement Predicted watch time

title: Models and Loss Functions Reference
heads: Deep  Cross Network — DCN (Google, 2017) → DCN v2 (2020)
All Loss Functions You Need to Know
text: # Problem Type → Baseline → Advanced Model Problem Type Baseline Advanced Binary classification (tabular) Logistic regression LightGBM / XGBoost → DNN Click prediction / ads ranking Logistic regression Wide Deep → DCN v2 Candidate retrieval (rec sys) Matrix factorization (ALS) Two-tower DNN + FAISS ANN Feed / search ranking LightGBM DCN v2, DLRM, MMoE (multi-task) Session-based recs Popularity baseline SASRec / BERT4Rec (Transformer) NLP: classification TF-IDF + LR Fine-tuned BERT / RoBERTa NLP: ranking / retrieval BM25 Bi-encoder (two-tower) → Cross-encoder Fraud detection LightGBM LightGBM + GNN (transaction graph) Image classification Linear on features ResNet → ViT Multimodal (text + image) Separate models, concat features CLIP-style dual encoder Time series / forecasting ARIMA, moving average LSTM → Temporal Fusion Transformer Graph problems (social, fraud) Node degree features + LR GraphSAGE, PinSage, GNN # Wide Deep vs. Deep Cross # Wide Deep (Google, 2016) Wide side : linear model on manually specified feature crosses (you write user_app × search_query ) Deep side : embedding + MLP for generalization Limitation : the cross features on the wide side must be hand-engineered When to use : you have strong domain knowledge about which specific interactions matter # Deep Cross Network — DCN (Google, 2017) → DCN v2 (2020) Replaces the wide side with a cross network that automatically learns bounded-degree feature interactions DCN v2 uses a matrix-based cross layer (more expressive than the original vector-based one) Reduces (not eliminates) manual cross engineering A strong upgrade over Wide Deep when you don t know which crosses matter When to use : large feature spaces, ranking problems where you don t know which crosses matter; a strong, common default for ranking, alongside DLRM/DeepFM # Summary Wide Deep → DCN → DCN v2 (manual crosses) (auto crosses, vector) (auto crosses, matrix — best) # All Loss Functions You Need to Know # Classification Binary Cross-Entropy (Log Loss) L = -[y·log(p) + (1-y)·log(1-p)] Use: click prediction, fraud, any binary label Output: sigmoid → probability Default choice for binary problems Categorical Cross-Entropy (Softmax Loss) L = -Σ y_i · log(p_i) Use: multi-class (mutually exclusive), intent detection, NLP classification Output: softmax → probability distribution Focal Loss L = -α_t (1-p_t)^γ · log(p_t) (p_t = probability assigned to the true class) Use: severe class imbalance (fraud, safety, object detection) The (1-p_t)^γ term downweights easy examples (of either class), focuses training on hard examples γ=2 is typical; originated in RetinaNet Often helps when easy negatives dominate; probabilities need recalibration # Regression MSE (Mean Squared Error) L = (y - ŷ)² Penalizes large errors heavily (squared) Sensitive to outliers Use: when large errors are disproportionately bad MAE (Mean Absolute Error) L = |y - ŷ| More robust to outliers than MSE Use: when outliers are common and you don t want them to dominate Huber Loss L = 0.5(y-ŷ)² if |y-ŷ| ≤ δ L = δ·|y-ŷ| - 0.5δ² otherwise Best of both: MSE for small errors, MAE for large ones Use: default regression loss when you re unsure (bid prediction, ETA) # Ranking BPR Loss (Bayesian Personalized Ranking) — pairwise L = -log(σ(ŷ_pos - ŷ_neg)) Pushes score of positive item above negative item Use: implicit feedback (clicks, watches) where you have user-item pairs Common in recommendation systems Hinge Loss — pairwise L = max(0, margin - (ŷ_pos - ŷ_neg)) Similar to BPR but with a hard margin Use: ranking when you want a minimum score gap LambdaRank / LambdaMART — listwise Pairwise gradients weighted by the NDCG change from swapping the pair (a listwise-aware heuristic); LambdaMART is the GBDT version Used inside LightGBM/XGBoost for ranking ( objective=lambdarank ) Use: when you care about the full ranked list quality, not just pairwise order ApproxNDCG / SoftNDCG — listwise Differentiable approximation of NDCG Used in neural ranking models Use: training neural rankers end-to-end # Embedding / Contrastive Triplet Loss L = max(0, d(anchor, pos) - d(anchor, neg) + margin) Pulls anchor closer to positive, pushes away from negative Use: face recognition, image similarity, early recommendation embedding work Problem: hard to mine good triplets NT-Xent Loss (SimCLR / Contrastive) L = -log( exp(sim(z_i, z_j)/τ) / Σ_k exp(sim(z_i, z_k)/τ) ) In-batch negatives: all other samples in the batch are negatives τ = temperature (lower = sharper, higher = softer) Use: self-supervised pretraining, two-tower models, sentence embeddings More efficient than triplet loss (no triplet mining needed) In-Batch Softmax (used in two-tower models) Same idea as NT-Xent but applied to user-item retrieval All other items in batch = negatives for each user Watch out: popular items appear often as negatives → popularity bias in training, correct with logQ correction (subtract log sampling probability from the logits) # Knowledge Distillation KL Divergence L = Σ p(x) · log(p(x)/q(x)) Measures how distribution p (teacher soft labels) differs from q (student predictions) Student loss = task loss + α·KL(teacher || student) Use: compressing large models to smaller ones for serving # Quick Lookup Situation Loss Binary, balanced Binary cross-entropy Binary, imbalanced (fraud, safety) Focal loss Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy Regression, clean data MSE Regression, noisy/outliers Huber or MAE Pairwise ranking (implicit feedback) BPR loss Listwise ranking (optimize NDCG) LambdaRank / ApproxNDCG Embedding learning NT-Xent (in-batch) or Triplet Model compression KL divergence Multi-task Weighted sum of per-task losses
